nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich Theorem
nodes.statement: If $L$ is an ordered vector space with the Riesz Decomposition Property and $M$ is a Dedekind complete vector lattice, then the ordered vector space $\blinop {L} {M}$ of order bounded linear operators between $L$ and $M$ is a Dedekind complete vector lattice. Moreover, if $S, T \in \blinop {L} {M}$, then for each $x \in L_+$ we have \begin {gather} [S \vee T] (x) = \sup \{S y + T (x - y) \mid 0 \leqslant y \leqslant x \}, \\ [S \wedge T] (x) = \inf \{S y + T (x - y) \mid 0 \leqslant y \leqslant x \}. \end {gather}
nodes.statement_short: Order bounded operators from an RDP space into a Dedekind complete vector lattice form a Dedekind complete vector lattice, with $\vee$ and $\wedge$ given by the Riesz-Kantorovich formulae.
nodes.origin_citation: M. Riesz 1940; L. V. Kantorovich 1936 (quoted from Aliprantis & Tourky 2002)
assumptions: $L$ is an ordered vector space with the Riesz Decomposition Property
$M$ is a Dedekind complete vector lattice
$S, T \in \blinop {L} {M}$
for each $x \in L_+$
conclusions: the ordered vector space $\blinop {L} {M}$ of order bounded linear operators between $L$ and $M$ is a Dedekind complete vector lattice
[S \vee T] (x) = \sup \{S y + T (x - y) \mid 0 \leqslant y \leqslant x \}
[S \wedge T] (x) = \inf \{S y + T (x - y) \mid 0 \leqslant y \leqslant x \}

nodes.name: Order bounded operators are regular
nodes.statement: In particular, this theorem implies that under its conditions every order bounded operator $T : L \to M$ is regular.
assumptions: under its conditions
conclusions: every order bounded operator $T : L \to M$ is regular

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich formulae
nodes.statement: Equations \eqref {stvee} and \eqref {stwedge} and their variants describing the lattice operations of $\blinop {L} {M}$ are known as the \emph {Riesz-Kantorovich formulae}.
differentia: describing the lattice operations of $\blinop {L} {M}$

nodes.name: Is an existing supremum of operators given by a Riesz-Kantorovich formula?
nodes.statement: Related to these formulae is the following long-standing problem that was posed in a number of slightly different versions (see, e.~g., \cite [\S 2] {positiveoperators}, \cite {aliprantistourky2002}): if a supremum of two linear opeartors $S, T \in \mathcal L$ exists in a linear space $\mathcal L$ of linear operators between $L$ and $M$ (where of special interest are the space of order bounded operators and the space of regular operators), is it given by a Riesz-Kantorovich formula?
nodes.statement_short: Long-standing question: when $\sup\{S,T\}$ exists in a space $\mathcal L$ of operators, is it given by the Riesz-Kantorovich formula?
nodes.origin_citation: posed in Aliprantis & Burkinshaw, Positive Operators, §2; Aliprantis & Tourky 2002

nodes.name: Contributions of the present work
nodes.statement: In the present work we extend the results of \cite {aliprantisetal2000} and \cite {aliprantistourky2002}. A direct approach, inspired by the well-known characterization of convex functions as supremums of sets of affine functions, allows us to get the complete answer in the case of order bounded functionals. Unfortunately, this method does not seem to give much information regarding the general case of order bounded linear operators acting from an ordered vector space $L$ into a Dedekind complete Riesz space $M$, which is geometrically far more challenging compared to the case of functionals $M = \mathbb R$. However, the same pattern still works to an extent if we assume that $L_+$ has an internal point and engage a natural extension of the Hahn-Banach theorem to construct suitable majorants. Although it only shows in this case that the Riesz-Kantorovich transform is linear on the set of internal points of $L_+$, leaving under question its linearity on the entire $L_+$, this is still sufficient for many applications. Moreover, this approach also allows us to characterize (under some additional assumptions) a generalization of the Riesz Decomposition Property of $L$ in terms of the Riesz Decomposition Property of $\blinop {L} {M}$ (as it was done, e.~g., in \cite {ando1962} for the duals of certain ordered Banach spaces) without much effort and without embedding the spaces into their second duals. We also give a characterization of conditions under which the Riesz-Kantorovich formulae are linear in terms of a generalization of the Riesz Decomposition Property and investigate certain conditions under which this generalization coincides with the (classical) Riesz Decomposition Property.
nodes.statement_short: The paper settles the functional case completely and, assuming $L_+$ has an internal point, handles operators via a Hahn-Banach extension, also characterising a generalised Riesz Decomposition Property.

nodes.name: Relaxation to a quasi-interior point
nodes.statement: To conclude the introduction, let us note that although the condition that $L_+$ has an interior point under which we give some answers regarding the case of the general space $M$ is a fairly strong assumption (e.~g. among the classical Banach lattices $\lclassg {p}$ only $\lclassg {\infty}$ satisfies it for all measures), it seems plausible nonetheless that at least under some suitable conditions it can be relaxed to the assumption that $L_+$ has a quasi-interior point (or a weak order unit; see, e.~g., \cite {borweinlewis1992}, \cite [Theorem 4.85] {positiveoperators1985}), which is often satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: The interior-point hypothesis on $L_+$ can plausibly be weakened to the existence of a quasi-interior point (weak order unit).
assumptions: the condition that $L_+$ has an interior point
conclusions: it seems plausible nonetheless that at least under some suitable conditions it can be relaxed to the assumption that $L_+$ has a quasi-interior point (or a weak order unit

nodes.name: ordered linear space (ordered vector space)
nodes.statement: An \emph {ordered linear space} $X$, also called an \emph {ordered vector space}, is a linear space (we only consider spaces over the field of reals $\mathbb R$) equipped with a partial order $\geqslant$ which is consistent with the linear structure, that is for all $x, y, z \in V$ such that $x \geqslant y$ and $\lambda \geqslant 0$ we have $x + z \geqslant y + z$ and $\lambda x \geqslant \lambda y$.
differentia: equipped with a partial order $\geqslant$ which is consistent with the linear structure

nodes.name: nonnegative cone $X_+$
nodes.statement: The order $\geqslant$ is completely determined by the \emph {nonnegative cone} $X_+ = \{x \in X \mid x \geqslant 0\}$ (which is a convex pointed cone) in the sense that every convex cone $K \subset X$ of a linear space $X$ such that $K \cap (-K) = \{0\}$ determines a unique order ($x \geqslant y$ if and only if $x - y \in K$) that turns $X$ into an ordered linear space satisfying $X_+ = K$.
nodes.statement_short: The order of $X$ corresponds bijectively to its cone $X_+$ of nonnegative elements.
differentia: $X_+ = \{x \in X \mid x \geqslant 0\}$

nodes.name: generating cone
nodes.statement: We say that a cone $X_+$ is \emph {generating in $X$} if $X = X_+ - X_+$, that is for any $x \in X$ there exist some $y, z \in X_+$ such that $x = y - z$.

nodes.name: order interval $[x,y]$
nodes.statement: An \emph {order interval} between a couple of points $x, y \in X$ such that $y \geqslant x$ is the set $[x, y] = \{ z \in X \mid x \leqslant z \leqslant y \}$.
differentia: $[x, y] = \{ z \in X \mid x \leqslant z \leqslant y \}$

nodes.name: order bounded set
nodes.statement: We say that a set $A \subset X$ is \emph {order bounded} if $A \subset [x, y]$ for some $x, y \in X$, $y \geqslant x$.
differentia: $A \subset [x, y]$ for some $x, y \in X$, $y \geqslant x$

nodes.name: upper bound
nodes.statement: If $y \geqslant x$ for all $x \in A$ then $y$ is called an \emph {upper bound} of $A$; we sometimes denote it by $y \geqslant A$.

nodes.name: supremum (least upper bound)
nodes.statement: If there exists some $x \in X$ such that $y \geqslant x$ for any upper bound $y$ of $A$, i.~e. if $x$ is the \emph {least upper bound} of $A$, then $x$ is called the \emph {supremum} of $A$ and we denote this fact by $x = \sup A$.

nodes.name: infimum
nodes.statement: Likewise, $x$ is called an \emph {infinum} of $A$, $x = \inf A$, if $x$ is the greatest lower bound. Naturally, it is equivalent to existence of the supremum $-x$ of the set $-A = \{-y \mid y \in A\}$, and we have $\inf A = -\sup (-A)$ in this case.

nodes.name: $\linop {X} {Y}$ and $\clinop {X} {Y}$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be linear spaces. We denote by $\linop {X} {Y}$ the set of all linear operators $T : X \to Y$. If, additionally, $X$ and $Y$ are equipped with topologies turning them into topological linear spaces, we denote by $\clinop {X} {Y} \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ the set of all continuous operators.

nodes.name: order bounded map
nodes.statement: We say that a (not necessarily linear) map $T : X \to Y$ is \emph {order bounded} if its values $T (A) = \{ T x \mid x \in A \}$ on order bounded sets $A \subset X$ are order bounded.
differentia: its values $T (A) = \{ T x \mid x \in A \}$ on order bounded sets $A \subset X$ are order bounded

nodes.name: positive and strictly positive maps
nodes.statement: $T$ is called \emph {positive} if $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in X_+$; we denote this fact by $T \geqslant 0$. $T$ is called \emph {strictly positive} if $T x > 0$ for all $x \in X_+ \setminus \{0\}$. We say that $S \geqslant T$ for some $S : X \to Y$ if $S - T \geqslant 0$; this defines a natural partial order on the set of all maps $T : X \to Y$.
differentia: $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in X_+$
$T x > 0$ for all $x \in X_+ \setminus \{0\}$

nodes.name: regular operator; $\blinop {X} {Y}$ and $\rlinop {X} {Y}$
nodes.statement: $T$ is called \emph {regular} if $T \in \linop {X} {Y}$ and $T = U - V$ for some positive $U, V \in \linop {X} {Y}$. We denote the set of order bounded linear operators between ordered linear spaces $X$ and $Y$ by $\blinop {X} {Y}$, and likewise the set of regular operators between $X$ and $Y$ by $\rlinop {X} {Y}$.
differentia: $T = U - V$ for some positive $U, V \in \linop {X} {Y}$

nodes.name: Why the order-dual notation is avoided
nodes.statement: It is customary to use the notation $\orderdual {X}$ for the \emph {order dual} $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ of an ordered linear space $X$; however, since the focus of the present work is spaces of general order bounded operators $\blinop {X} {Y}$ this notation might be a bit confusing, so we will avoid it.

nodes.name: Positive linear operators are order bounded
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that every positive linear operator is order bounded and thus $\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \blinop {X} {Y}$; this inclusion may be proper in general.
conclusions: It is easy to see that every positive linear operator is order bounded and thus $\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \blinop {X} {Y}$; this inclusion may be proper in general.

nodes.name: Lexicographic order has a one-dimensional dual
nodes.statement: Both of these sets of operators may be very narrow: for example, if $X = \mathbb R^2$ is the plane with the lexicographic order $X_+ = \left\{ (x, y) \mid \text {either $y > 0$ or $y = 0$ and $x \geqslant 0$} \right\}$ then $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} = \blinop {X} {\mathbb R} = \{f \mid f (x, y) = \alpha y \}$, and in general ordered linear spaces with the lexicographic order have one-dimensional duals $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} = \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ irrespective to the (finite or infinite) dimension of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: For the lexicographically ordered plane the regular and order bounded duals both collapse to the one-dimensional space $\{f \mid f(x,y) = \alpha y\}$.

nodes.name: superadditive and additive maps
nodes.statement: A map $T : X_+ \to Y$ is called \emph {superadditive} if $T (x + y) \geqslant T (x) + T (y)$ for all $x, y \in X_+$; $T$ is called \emph {additive} if $T (x + y) = T (x) + T (y)$ for all $x, y \in X_+$.
differentia: $T (x + y) \geqslant T (x) + T (y)$ for all $x, y \in X_+$

nodes.name: superlinear and linear maps on a cone
nodes.statement: If, in addition, $T$ is \emph {positively homogeneous}, that is $T (\lambda x) = \lambda T (x)$ for all $\lambda \geqslant 0$ and $x \in X_+$, we say that $T$ is \emph {superlinear} and \emph {linear} respectively.
differentia: $T (\lambda x) = \lambda T (x)$ for all $\lambda \geqslant 0$ and $x \in X_+$

nodes.name: Unique linear extension from a generating cone
nodes.statement: If the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$ then any linear map $T : X_+ \to Y$ can be uniquely extended to a linear map on all $X$ by setting $T x = T y - T z$ for $x = y - z$, $x \in X$, $y, z \in X_+$.
conclusions: If the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$ then any linear map $T : X_+ \to Y$ can be uniquely extended to a linear map on all $X$ by setting $T x = T y - T z$ for $x = y - z$, $x \in X$, $y, z \in X_+$.

nodes.name: $\suplinop {X_+} {Y}$, the space of superlinear maps
nodes.statement: We denote the set of all superlinear maps $T : X_+ \to Y$ by \suplinop {X_+} {Y}.

nodes.name: Riesz Decomposition Property
nodes.statement: An ordered linear space $X$ is said to satisfy the \emph {Riesz Decomposition Property} if $[0, x] + [0, y] = [0, x + y]$ for all $x, y \in X_+$; here and elsewhere a sum of sets $A$ and $B$ in a linear space is the Minkowski sum $A + B = \{a + b \mid a \in A, \,\, b \in B\}$.

nodes.name: interpolation property
nodes.statement: It is well known that the Riesz Decomposition Property is equivalent to the \emph {interpolation property}: for any finite $A, B \subset X$ such that $A \leqslant B$ in the sense that $a \leqslant b$ for all $a \in A$ and $b \in B$ there exists some $x \in X$ such that $A \leqslant x \leqslant B$, i.~e. $a \leqslant x \leqslant b$ for all $a \in A$ and $b \in B$.
nodes.statement_short: RDP is equivalent to the interpolation property: any finite $A \leqslant B$ can be separated by some $x$ with $A \leqslant x \leqslant B$.

nodes.name: lattice (Riesz space)
nodes.statement: An ordered linear space $X$ is said to be a \emph {lattice} or \emph {Riesz space} if for any $x, y \in X$ the supremum $x \vee y = \sup \{x, y\}$ exists in $X$. If this is the case then infinums $x \wedge y = -[(-x) \vee (-y)]$, positive parts $x^+ = x \vee 0$ and moduli $|x| = x \vee (-x)$ also exist.
differentia: for any $x, y \in X$ the supremum $x \vee y = \sup \{x, y\}$ exists in $X$

nodes.name: A lattice has the Riesz Decomposition Property
nodes.statement: A lattice always has the Riesz Decomposition Property.
conclusions: A lattice always has the Riesz Decomposition Property.

nodes.name: Dedekind complete ordered linear space
nodes.statement: An ordered linear space $X$ is called \emph {Dedekind complete} (or just \emph {complete}) if any set $A \subset X$ that has an upper bound also has a supremum $\sup A$.
differentia: any set $A \subset X$ that has an upper bound also has a supremum

nodes.name: Hahn-Banach Theorem (superlinear-minorant form)
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, $Y$ is Dedekind complete, $L \subset X$ is a linear space such that $X_+ + L = X$, $p : X_+ \to Y$ is a superlinear map and $T_0 : L \to Y$ is a linear operator satisfying $T_0 x \geqslant p (x)$ for all $x \in L \cap X_+$. Then there exists an extension $T \in \linop {X} {Y}$ of $T_0$ satisfying $T x \geqslant p (x)$ for all $x \in X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: A linear operator on $L$ dominating a superlinear $p$ on $L \cap X_+$ extends to all of $X$ while still dominating $p$ on $X_+$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces
$Y$ is Dedekind complete
$L \subset X$ is a linear space such that $X_+ + L = X$
$p : X_+ \to Y$ is a superlinear map
$T_0 : L \to Y$ is a linear operator satisfying $T_0 x \geqslant p (x)$ for all $x \in L \cap X_+$
conclusions: there exists an extension $T \in \linop {X} {Y}$ of $T_0$ satisfying $T x \geqslant p (x)$ for all $x \in X_+$

nodes.name: Sublinear majorants, Hahn-Banach-Kantorovich and M. Riesz extension
nodes.statement: This theorem is nearly always formulated with sublinear majorants $q = -p$, but superlinear minorants suit the purposes of the present work better. Setting $X_+ = X$ (i.~e. considering the full order, that is $x \geqslant y$ for all $x, y \in X$; the assumption that $X_+$ is a partial order is not actually used) yields what is often called the Hahn-Banach-Kantorovich theorem (\cite {kantorovich1935}); letting $p = 0$ produces the M.~Riesz extension theorem (\cite {riesz1923}).
nodes.statement_short: Taking $X_+ = X$ gives the Hahn-Banach-Kantorovich theorem and $p = 0$ gives the M. Riesz extension theorem.

nodes.name: Proof of the Hahn-Banach Theorem (sketch)
nodes.statement: Let us give a sketch of the proof. By the standard inductive reasoning it is sufficient to consider the case $\dim X \slash L = 1$. We fix some $x_0 \in X \setminus L$; then $X = \{x + s x_0 \mid x \in L, s \in \mathbb R\}$ and we need to define a value $y_0 \in Y$ in such a way that an extension $T (x + s x_0) = T_0 x + s y_0$ would satisfy the necessary estimate $T (x + s x_0) \geqslant p (x + s x_0)$ whenever $x + s x_0 \in X_+$. Considering different signs of $s$ we see that this is equivalent to \begin {equation} T_0 u - p (u - x_0) \geqslant y_0 \geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v \end {equation} for all $u, v \in L$ satisfying $u - x_0 \in X_+$ and $v + x_0 \in X_+$. Observe that such $u$ and $v$ always exist since by the assumptions $$ X_+ + L = X = -X = -(X_+ + L) = -X_+ - L = -X_+ + L, $$ and for any such $u$ and $v$ we have $u + v = (u - x_0) + (v + x_0) \in X_+ \cap L$, so $$ T_0 u + T_0 v = T_0 (u + v) \geqslant p (u + v) = p ([u - x_0] + [v + x_0]) \geqslant p (u - x_0) + p (v + x_0) $$ by superlinearity of $p$, which implies that \begin {equation} T_0 u - p (u - x_0) \geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v \end {equation} for any $u, v \in L$ satisfying $u - x_0 \in X_+$ and $v + x_0 \in X_+$. From \eqref {hbk1} it is clear that the set of values of the right-hand part of~\eqref {hbk} has an upper bound, and the least upper bound of the right-hand part is also a lower bound for the left-hand part. Thus we may set $$ y_0 = \sup \{p (v + x_0) - T_0 v \mid v + x_0 \in X_+\} $$ and conclude that $y_0$ satisfies the required estimates~\eqref {hbk}.
nodes.statement_short: Induct down to a codimension-one extension, then take $y_0$ to be the supremum of the lower bounds forced by superlinearity of $p$.

nodes.name: Reduce to codimension one
nodes.statement: By the standard inductive reasoning it is sufficient to consider the case $\dim X \slash L = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Standard inductive reasoning reduces the statement to the case $\dim X \slash L = 1$.

nodes.name: Parametrise the extension
nodes.statement: We fix some $x_0 \in X \setminus L$; then $X = \{x + s x_0 \mid x \in L, s \in \mathbb R\}$ and we need to define a value $y_0 \in Y$ in such a way that an extension $T (x + s x_0) = T_0 x + s y_0$ would satisfy the necessary estimate $T (x + s x_0) \geqslant p (x + s x_0)$ whenever $x + s x_0 \in X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $x_0 \notin L$; extending $T_0$ amounts to choosing a single value $y_0 \in Y$.

nodes.name: Split on the sign of $s$
nodes.statement: Considering different signs of $s$ we see that this is equivalent to \begin {equation} T_0 u - p (u - x_0) \geqslant y_0 \geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v \end {equation} for all $u, v \in L$ satisfying $u - x_0 \in X_+$ and $v + x_0 \in X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Splitting on the sign of $s$ turns the required estimate into a two-sided bound on $y_0$.

nodes.name: Admissible $u,v$ exist and interlace
nodes.statement: Observe that such $u$ and $v$ always exist since by the assumptions $$ X_+ + L = X = -X = -(X_+ + L) = -X_+ - L = -X_+ + L, $$ and for any such $u$ and $v$ we have $u + v = (u - x_0) + (v + x_0) \in X_+ \cap L$, so $$ T_0 u + T_0 v = T_0 (u + v) \geqslant p (u + v) = p ([u - x_0] + [v + x_0]) \geqslant p (u - x_0) + p (v + x_0) $$ by superlinearity of $p$, which implies that \begin {equation} T_0 u - p (u - x_0) \geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v \end {equation} for any $u, v \in L$ satisfying $u - x_0 \in X_+$ and $v + x_0 \in X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Show admissible $u, v$ exist and, by superlinearity of $p$, that the lower bounds never exceed the upper bounds.

nodes.name: Take the least upper bound
nodes.statement: From \eqref {hbk1} it is clear that the set of values of the right-hand part of~\eqref {hbk} has an upper bound, and the least upper bound of the right-hand part is also a lower bound for the left-hand part. Thus we may set $$ y_0 = \sup \{p (v + x_0) - T_0 v \mid v + x_0 \in X_+\} $$ and conclude that $y_0$ satisfies the required estimates~\eqref {hbk}.
nodes.statement_short: Set $y_0$ to the supremum of the lower bounds and check it satisfies the required estimates.

nodes.name: internal point (core point)
nodes.statement: We say that $e \in A$ is an \emph {internal point} of a set $A \subset X$ (sometimes also called a \emph {core point} or an \emph {algebraically interior point}) if for any $x \in A$ there exists some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $e + \alpha x \in A$ for all values $\alpha \in \mathbb R$ satisfying $-\varepsilon < \alpha < \varepsilon$. We denote the set of internal points of $A$ by $\tint A$.
differentia: for any $x \in A$ there exists some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $e + \alpha x \in A$ for all values $\alpha \in \mathbb R$ satisfying $-\varepsilon < \alpha < \varepsilon$

nodes.name: line-open set
nodes.statement: It is well known that this notion of an internal point has a lot in common with the usual topological notion of an interior point. With only a limited number of caveats the \emph {line-open sets} $A$, i.~e. the sets $A \subset X$ such that $A = \tint A$, behave very much like open sets in a Hausdorff linear topological space.
differentia: the sets $A \subset X$ such that $A = \tint A$

nodes.name: Convex combinations with an internal point are internal
nodes.statement: A convex combination $(1 - \theta) y + \theta x$, $0 < \theta < 1$, of an internal point $x \in \tint A$ of $A$ and some $y \in A$ is also an internal point of $A$.
conclusions: A convex combination $(1 - \theta) y + \theta x$, $0 < \theta < 1$, of an internal point $x \in \tint A$ of $A$ and some $y \in A$ is also an internal point of $A$.

nodes.name: order unit
nodes.statement: A vector $e \in X_+$ is called an \emph {order unit} of $X$ if for any $x \in X$ there exists some $\lambda > 0$ such that $x \leqslant \lambda e$.
differentia: for any $x \in X$ there exists some $\lambda > 0$ such that $x \leqslant \lambda e$

nodes.name: Order units are exactly the internal points of $X_+$
nodes.statement: It is well known that $e$ is an order unit of $X$ if and only if $e$ is an internal point of $X_+$.
conclusions: It is well known that $e$ is an order unit of $X$ if and only if $e$ is an internal point of $X_+$.

nodes.name: order topology
nodes.statement: The \emph {order topology} of $X$ is the finest locally convex topology that has a base of convex circled open neighbourhoods at $0$ that absorb every order interval of $X$; this topology is Hausdorff if and only if $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ separates points of $X$ (i.~e. if and only if $f (x) = 0$ for all $f \in \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ implies $x = 0$).
nodes.statement_short: The finest locally convex topology whose neighbourhoods of $0$ absorb every order interval; it is Hausdorff exactly when $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ separates points.
nodes.origin_citation: Namioka 1957; Schaefer 1958; Aliprantis & Tourky, Cones and Duality
differentia: has a base of convex circled open neighbourhoods at $0$ that absorb every order interval of $X$

nodes.name: Order bounded functionals are exactly the order-continuous ones
nodes.statement: An important property of the order topology is that $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R} = \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ (see, e.~g., \cite [Theorem~2.69] {conesandduality}).
nodes.origin_citation: Aliprantis & Tourky, Cones and Duality, Theorem 2.69
conclusions: An important property of the order topology is that $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R} = \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ (see, e.~g., \cite [Theorem~2.69] {conesandduality}).

nodes.name: $f$ separates $x$ from $A$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is a linear space, $Y$ is an ordered linear space, $A \subset X$ is a convex set, $x \in X$ and $f \in \linop {X} {Y}$. We say that \emph {$f$ separates $x$ from $A$} if either $f (x) \leqslant f (A)$ or $f (x) \geqslant f (A)$, where $f (A) = \{f (y) \mid y \in A\}$.
differentia: either $f (x) \leqslant f (A)$ or $f (x) \geqslant f (A)$

nodes.name: $f$ strictly separates $x$ from $A$
nodes.statement: Suppose also that $Y$ is Dedekind complete. We say that \emph {$f$ strictly separates $x$ from $A$} if $f$ separates $x$ from $A$ and the appropriate condition is strengthened as either $f (x) < \inf f (A)$ or $f (x) > \sup f (A)$. In the case $Y = \mathbb R$ these properties coincide with the usual separation (either strict or non-strict) by a linear functional.
differentia: the appropriate condition is strengthened as either $f (x) < \inf f (A)$ or $f (x) > \sup f (A)$

nodes.name: $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, $Y$ is Dedekind complete and $\mathcal L$ is a linear subspace of $\linop {X} {Y}$. We say that $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property if for any $x, y \in X_+$ and $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus ([0, x] + [0, y])$ point $z$ cannot be strictly separated from $[0, x] + [0, y]$ by a map from $\mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-RDP if no point of $[0,x+y]$ outside $[0,x]+[0,y]$ can be strictly separated from that sum by a map of $\mathcal L$.
differentia: for any $x, y \in X_+$ and $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus ([0, x] + [0, y])$ point $z$ cannot be strictly separated from $[0, x] + [0, y]$ by a map from $\mathcal L$

nodes.name: RDP implies the $\mathcal L$-RDP
nodes.statement: Trivially, if $X$ satisfies the Riesz Decomposition Property then it satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property with any $\mathcal L$.
conclusions: Trivially, if $X$ satisfies the Riesz Decomposition Property then it satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property with any $\mathcal L$.

nodes.name: The $\mathcal L$-RDP is strictly weaker than the RDP
nodes.statement: On the other hand, however, it is easy to construct an example that shows that the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property is weaker than the Riesz Decomposition Property for $Y = \mathbb R$ and the widest possible space $\mathcal L = \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$. We will now give a detailed description of such an example; see Figure~\ref {figrdpex}.

nodes.name: An order on $\mathbb R^3$ with the $\mathcal L$-RDP but not the RDP
nodes.statement: Let $X = \mathbb R^3$ and $X_+ = \{ (x, y, z) \mid \text {$x, y, z > 0$ or $z = 0$, $x = y \geqslant 0$}\}$. Observe that order interval $[0, (2, 1, 1)]$ is the union of an open rectangular box $ \{(x, y, z) \mid 0 < x < 2, \,\, 0 < y < 1, \,\, 0 < z < 1\} $ and two parallel semiopen segments connecting $(0, 0, 0)$ with $(1, 1, 0)$ not including $(1, 1, 0)$ and $(2, 1, 1)$ with $(1, 0, 1)$ not including $(1, 0, 1)$. The order interval $[0, (1, 2, 1)]$ has similar structure because it is the mirror image of $[0, (2, 1, 1)]$ with respect to the symmetry plane $\{(x, y, z) \mid x = y \}$ of $X_+$. It is easy to see that $ [0, (2, 1, 1) + (1, 2, 1)] = [0, (3, 3, 2)] $ is the union of an open rectangular box $$ \{(x, y, z) \mid 0 < x < 3, \,\, 0 < y < 3, \,\, 0 < z < 2\} $$ and two parallel semiopen segments connecting $(0, 0, 0)$ with $(3, 3, 0)$ not including $(3, 3, 0)$ and $(3, 3, 2)$ with $(0, 0, 2)$ not including $(0, 0, 2)$. Thus $[0, (3, 3, 2)] \setminus \left([0, (2, 1, 1)] + [0, (1, 2, 1)]\right)$ is a union of a semiopen segment between $(0, 0, 3)$ and $(1, 1, 3)$ not including $(0, 0, 3)$ and a semiopen segment between $(2, 2, 0)$ and $(3, 3, 0)$ not including $(3, 3, 0)$, and so $X$ does not satisfy the Riesz Decomposition Property. However, observe that the closure of the order intervals $[0, a]$, $a \in X_+$ (in the standard topology of $\mathbb R^3$, which is the only topology there is that turns $\mathbb R^3$ into a Hausdorff linear topological space) coincides with the order intervals of $\mathbb R^3$ ordered by the standard cone $$ \mathbb R^3_+ = \{(x, y, z) \mid x \geqslant 0, \,\, y \geqslant 0, \,\, z \geqslant 0 \} $$ with which $\mathbb R^3$ is a lattice and thus has the Riesz Decomposition Property. Therefore for all $a, b \in X_+$ the set $[0, a + b] \setminus \left([0, a] + [0, b]\right)$ lies in the closure of $[0, a + b]$. Since $X$ is finite dimensional, every functional from $\mathcal L$ is continuous and therefore cannot strictly separate a convex set from a point in its closure. Thus $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property for any $\mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: A cone in $\mathbb R^3$ whose order intervals differ from their closures only on boundary segments: RDP fails, yet the $\mathcal L$-RDP holds for every $\mathcal L$.

nodes.name: How much weaker the $\mathcal L$-RDP can be
nodes.statement: Of course, if the set $\mathcal L$ is very small with respect to $\linop {X} {Y}$ in a certain sense, for example if $X$ is infinite-dimensional and all operators from $\mathcal L$ factor through a finite-dimensional space, then the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property may be \emph {much} more general than the Riesz Decomposition Property; an obvious example is that \emph {any} couple of ordered linear spaces $X$, $Y$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property if all operators from $\mathcal L$ factor through a one-dimensional space, or just $\mathcal L = \{0\}$. On the other hand, it is easy to enumerate a number of cases where both properties are actually equivalent based on various separation theorems; let us give a couple of examples.
nodes.statement_short: If all maps of $\mathcal L$ factor through a one-dimensional space the $\mathcal L$-RDP is vacuous; separation theorems give cases where the two properties coincide.

nodes.name: RDP equals the continuous-functional RDP for compact order intervals
nodes.statement: Suppose that ordered linear space $X$ is equipped with a topology that turns it into a locally convex Hausdorff linear space and order intervals $[0, x]$ are compact for any $x \in X_+$. Then $X$ satisfies the Riesz Decomposition Property if and only if $X$ satisfies the $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$-Riesz Decomposition Property.
nodes.statement_short: With compact order intervals in a locally convex Hausdorff space, RDP and the $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$-RDP are equivalent.
assumptions: ordered linear space $X$ is equipped with a topology that turns it into a locally convex Hausdorff linear space
order intervals $[0, x]$ are compact for any $x \in X_+$
conclusions: $X$ satisfies the Riesz Decomposition Property if and only if $X$ satisfies the $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$-Riesz Decomposition Property

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition rdplrdp
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that $X$ satisfies the $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$-Riesz Decomposition Property under the conditions of Proposition~\ref {rdplrdp} and there exist some $x, y \in X_+$ and $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left( [0, x] + [0, y] \right)$. $[0, x] + [0, y]$ is a compact convex set because it is the Minkowski sum of two compact convex sets. Then by a standard separation theorem $z$ can be strictly separated from $[0, x] + [0, y]$ by some $f \in \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a failure of RDP gives a point outside a compact convex Minkowski sum, which a standard separation theorem separates strictly.

nodes.name: Assume RDP fails
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that $X$ satisfies the $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$-Riesz Decomposition Property under the conditions of Proposition~\ref {rdplrdp} and there exist some $x, y \in X_+$ and $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left( [0, x] + [0, y] \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$-RDP holds but RDP fails, giving a point $z$ outside $[0,x]+[0,y]$.

nodes.name: Minkowski sum is compact convex
nodes.statement: $[0, x] + [0, y]$ is a compact convex set because it is the Minkowski sum of two compact convex sets.
nodes.statement_short: Note $[0,x]+[0,y]$ is compact and convex as a Minkowski sum of two such sets.

nodes.name: Separate and contradict
nodes.statement: Then by a standard separation theorem $z$ can be strictly separated from $[0, x] + [0, y]$ by some $f \in \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: A standard separation theorem strictly separates $z$ by a continuous functional, contradicting the hypothesis.

nodes.name: base of a cone
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space and $B \subset X$ is a convex set. We say that a cone $X_+$ \emph {has a base $B$} if for any $x \in X_+ \setminus \{0\}$ there exist unique $y \in B$ and $\lambda > 0$ such that $x = \lambda y$; for details on cones with bases see, e.~g., \cite [Section~1.7] {conesandduality}.
differentia: for any $x \in X_+ \setminus \{0\}$ there exist unique $y \in B$ and $\lambda > 0$ such that $x = \lambda y$

nodes.name: Bases correspond to strictly positive functionals
nodes.statement: Existence of a base for $X_+$ is equiuvalent to existence of a strictly positive functional $f$ in $X$; in this case the set $B = \{ x \in X_+ \mid f (x) = 1\}$ is a base for $X_+$.
conclusions: Existence of a base for $X_+$ is equiuvalent to existence of a strictly positive functional $f$ in $X$; in this case the set $B = \{ x \in X_+ \mid f (x) = 1\}$ is a base for $X_+$.

nodes.name: Restrictions to a base are exactly the affine functionals
nodes.statement: Restrictions of maps from $\linop {X} {Y}$ on $B$ are exactly the affine functionals on $B$ taking values in $Y$, and restrictions $K \cap B$ of convex cones $K \subset X_+$ are exactly the convex subsets of $B$.
conclusions: Restrictions of maps from $\linop {X} {Y}$ on $B$ are exactly the affine functionals on $B$ taking values in $Y$, and restrictions $K \cap B$ of convex cones $K \subset X_+$ are exactly the convex subsets of $B$.

nodes.name: bounded aperture on parallel lines
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an ordered linear space such that the cone $X_+$ has a base $B$. We say that $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines if for any $x \in X$ there exists some $c_x \geqslant 0$ such that for any $y \in B \setminus \{x\}$ the length of the intersection $B \cap \ell$ is at most $c_x$, where $\ell$ is the line passing through points $y$ and $x + y$.
nodes.statement_short: Along every parallel-line direction the chords of a base $B$ have uniformly bounded length.
differentia: for any $x \in X$ there exists some $c_x \geqslant 0$ such that for any $y \in B \setminus \{x\}$ the length of the intersection $B \cap \ell$ is at most $c_x$

nodes.name: Bounded aperture does not depend on the base
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to consider only points $x$ from the affine hull of $B$ in Definition~\ref {finap}, since otherwise $B \cap \ell$ is a single point. Also, since all bases of a cone are affinely isomorphic and affine maps preserve relative lengths of parallel segments, Definition~\ref {finap} does not depend on a particular choice of a base $B$.

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional characterisation of bounded aperture
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that for the finite dimensional ordered spaces the cone $X_+$ has bounded aperture if and only if its closure does not contain any lines, i.~e. one-dimensional spaces.
conclusions: It is easy to see that for the finite dimensional ordered spaces the cone $X_+$ has bounded aperture if and only if its closure does not contain any lines, i.~e. one-dimensional spaces.

nodes.name: A compact base implies bounded aperture
nodes.statement: It is also easy to see that if $X$ is a Hausdorff ordered linear topological space such that the cone $X_+$ has a compact base $B$ then the cone $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines; however, this property seems to be much weaker than any kind of compactness.
conclusions: It is also easy to see that if $X$ is a Hausdorff ordered linear topological space such that the cone $X_+$ has a compact base $B$ then the cone $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines; however, this property seems to be much weaker than any kind of compactness.

nodes.name: Bounded convex base in an infinite-dimensional normed space
nodes.statement: For example, if $B$ is a bounded convex set in an infinite dimensional normed linear space then the cone $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines (since the length of $B \cap \ell$ in Definition~\ref {finap} is proportional to $\|z_0 - z_1\|$, where $z_0$ and $z_1$ are the endpoints of $B \cap \ell$), but at the same time $B$ may lack any meaningful kind of compactness.
nodes.statement_short: A norm-bounded convex base gives bounded aperture without any compactness.

nodes.name: Separation of cones by a regular functional
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$ and $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines. Let $K_0, K_1 \subset X_+$ be two nonempty convex cones such that $K_0 \cap K_1 = \emptyset$ and $\tint K_0 \neq \emptyset$. Then there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, $f \neq 0$, such that $f$ separates $K_0$ and $K_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Disjoint convex subcones of $X_+$, one with an internal point, can be separated by a nonzero regular functional.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$ and $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines
$K_0, K_1 \subset X_+$ be two nonempty convex cones such that $K_0 \cap K_1 = \emptyset$ and $\tint K_0 \neq \emptyset$
conclusions: there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, $f \neq 0$, such that $f$ separates $K_0$ and $K_1$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition regfuncsep
nodes.statement: Indeed, let $B$ be a base of the cone $X_+$, let $L$ be the affine hull of $B$ and let $A_j = K_j \cap B$ for $j \in \{0, 1\}$. Then $\tint A_0 \neq \emptyset$ as a subset of $L$ (for the rest of the proof we denote by $\tint D$ the sets of internal points of $D \subset L$ in $L$ rather than in $X$), and by the standard separation theorem there exists a linear functional $h_{00} \in \linop {L} {\mathbb R}$ separating $A_0$ and $A_1$. This means that for some $\alpha \in \mathbb R$ the hyperplane $H = \{y \in L \mid h_{00} (y) = \alpha\}$ separates $A_0$ and $A_1$ in $L$. Let $x_0 \in \tint A_0$ and let $y_0 \in H \cap B$; then $x_0 \notin H$. Space $L$ can then be parametrized as $L = \{s (x_0 - y_0) + y \mid s \in \mathbb R, y \in H \}$. By the bounded aperture property assumption there exists some $c \in \mathbb R$ such that \begin {equation} B \subset \{s (x_0 - y_0) + y \mid |s| \leqslant c, \,\, y \in H \}. \end {equation} Let us define two affine functionals for $z = s (x_0 - y_0) + y$, $s \in \mathbb R$, $y \in H$ by $h_0 (z) = 1 + \frac 1 {2 c} s$ and $h_1 (z) = 1 - \frac 1 {2 c} s$, and let $f_0, f_1 \in \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ be the unique linear extensions of $h_0$ and $h_1$. \eqref {positiveonb} implies that $h_0$ and $h_1$ are positive on $B$, so we have $f_0, f_1 \geqslant 0$ and thus $f = f_0 - f_1$ is a regular functional that is a unique extension of $h = h_0 - h_1$. By construction $h$ is an affine functional that defines the same hyperplane $H$, i.~e. $H = \{y \in L \mid h (y) = 0 \}$, and it is easy to see that we also have $h (A_0) \leqslant 0$ and $h (A_1) \geqslant 0$, so $h$ separates $A_0$ and $A_1$, and therefore $f$ separates $K_0$ and $K_1$. The proof of Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Separate inside a base by a standard theorem, then use bounded aperture to write the separating affine functional as a difference of two positive ones.

nodes.name: Pass to a base
nodes.statement: Indeed, let $B$ be a base of the cone $X_+$, let $L$ be the affine hull of $B$ and let $A_j = K_j \cap B$ for $j \in \{0, 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the cones to a base $B$ of $X_+$ and work inside its affine hull $L$.

nodes.name: Separate inside the base
nodes.statement: Then $\tint A_0 \neq \emptyset$ as a subset of $L$ (for the rest of the proof we denote by $\tint D$ the sets of internal points of $D \subset L$ in $L$ rather than in $X$), and by the standard separation theorem there exists a linear functional $h_{00} \in \linop {L} {\mathbb R}$ separating $A_0$ and $A_1$. This means that for some $\alpha \in \mathbb R$ the hyperplane $H = \{y \in L \mid h_{00} (y) = \alpha\}$ separates $A_0$ and $A_1$ in $L$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the standard separation theorem in $L$ to get a hyperplane $H$ separating $A_0$ and $A_1$.

nodes.name: Parametrise $L$
nodes.statement: Let $x_0 \in \tint A_0$ and let $y_0 \in H \cap B$; then $x_0 \notin H$. Space $L$ can then be parametrized as $L = \{s (x_0 - y_0) + y \mid s \in \mathbb R, y \in H \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $x_0 \in \tint A_0$ and $y_0 \in H \cap B$ and parametrise $L$ along the direction $x_0 - y_0$.

nodes.name: Bound the base along the direction
nodes.statement: By the bounded aperture property assumption there exists some $c \in \mathbb R$ such that \begin {equation} B \subset \{s (x_0 - y_0) + y \mid |s| \leqslant c, \,\, y \in H \}. \end {equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bounded aperture confines $B$ to a slab $|s| \leqslant c$ in this parametrisation.

nodes.name: Build two positive functionals
nodes.statement: Let us define two affine functionals for $z = s (x_0 - y_0) + y$, $s \in \mathbb R$, $y \in H$ by $h_0 (z) = 1 + \frac 1 {2 c} s$ and $h_1 (z) = 1 - \frac 1 {2 c} s$, and let $f_0, f_1 \in \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ be the unique linear extensions of $h_0$ and $h_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $h_0 = 1 + s/(2c)$ and $h_1 = 1 - s/(2c)$ and extend them linearly to $X$.

nodes.name: Their difference is regular
nodes.statement: \eqref {positiveonb} implies that $h_0$ and $h_1$ are positive on $B$, so we have $f_0, f_1 \geqslant 0$ and thus $f = f_0 - f_1$ is a regular functional that is a unique extension of $h = h_0 - h_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Both extensions are positive, so $f = f_0 - f_1$ is a regular functional.

nodes.name: It separates the cones
nodes.statement: By construction $h$ is an affine functional that defines the same hyperplane $H$, i.~e. $H = \{y \in L \mid h (y) = 0 \}$, and it is easy to see that we also have $h (A_0) \leqslant 0$ and $h (A_1) \geqslant 0$, so $h$ separates $A_0$ and $A_1$, and therefore $f$ separates $K_0$ and $K_1$. The proof of Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: $h = h_0 - h_1$ defines the same hyperplane $H$, hence $f$ separates $K_0$ and $K_1$.

nodes.name: Bounded aperture cannot be dropped
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to see that the assumption that $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines cannot be dropped from Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep}: if the affine hull of the base $B$ of $X_+$ contains a line $\ell$, then any positive functional $f_0$ has to be constant on $\ell$, and thus no $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, $f \neq 0$, can separate any cones $K_0, K_1 \subset X_+$ such that $\ell \cap \tint K_j \neq \emptyset$ for $j \in \{0, 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: If the affine hull of the base contains a line, positive functionals are constant on it and no regular functional can separate.

nodes.name: Every hyperplane is defined by a regular functional
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$, $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines and $\tint X_+ \neq \emptyset$. Let $H \subset X$ be a hyperplane. Then there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $H = \{x \mid f (x) = \alpha\}$ with some $\alpha \in \mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: Under bounded aperture and a nonempty cone interior, every hyperplane is a level set of a regular functional.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$, $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines and $\tint X_+ \neq \emptyset$
$H \subset X$ be a hyperplane
conclusions: there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $H = \{x \mid f (x) = \alpha\}$ with some $\alpha \in \mathbb R$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition regfunchp
nodes.statement: First, fix any $x_0 \in H$, and let $H_0 = H - x_0$; we want to find some $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $H_0 = \{x \mid f (x) = 0\}$. Let $h_0 \in \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ be a (not necessarily regular) linear functional defining $H_0$, that is $H_0 = \{x \mid h_0 (x) = 0\}$. If $H_0 \cap X_+ = \{0\}$ then either $h_0$ or $-h_0$ is positive and we can put $f = h_0$ right away. Otherwise let $$ K_0 = \{x \in X_+ \mid h_0 (x) < 0\} $$ and $$ K_1 = \{x \in X_+ \mid h_0 (x) > 0\}. $$ By assumptions there exists some $z \in \tint X_+$. We may assume that $z \notin H_0$, since otherwise we may replace $z$ with a convex combination of $z$ and some point in $X_+ \setminus H_0$ (we cannot have $X_+ \subset H_0$ since $X_+$ is assumed to be generating in $X$). Therefore $$ z \in K_j = \{h_0 < 0\} \cap \tint X_+ = \tint K_j $$ for some $j \in \{0, 1\}$; by changing the sign of $h_0$ we may thus assume that $\tint K_0 \neq \emptyset$. Applying Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep} yields a functional $f_0 \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ separating $K_0$ and $K_1$, and since the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$, it is easy to see that $H_0 = \{ x \mid f (x) = 0\}$. Finally, $H = \{x \mid f (x) = f (x_0)\}$, and the proof of Proposition~\ref {regfunchp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Translate $H$ to a subspace, split into the trivial and nontrivial cases, and separate the two half-cones by the previous proposition.

nodes.name: Translate to a subspace
nodes.statement: First, fix any $x_0 \in H$, and let $H_0 = H - x_0$; we want to find some $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $H_0 = \{x \mid f (x) = 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate $H$ so that it becomes a linear subspace $H_0$ through the origin.

nodes.name: Pick a defining functional
nodes.statement: Let $h_0 \in \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ be a (not necessarily regular) linear functional defining $H_0$, that is $H_0 = \{x \mid h_0 (x) = 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take any linear functional $h_0$ defining $H_0$.

nodes.name: Trivial case and half-cones
nodes.statement: If $H_0 \cap X_+ = \{0\}$ then either $h_0$ or $-h_0$ is positive and we can put $f = h_0$ right away. Otherwise let $$ K_0 = \{x \in X_+ \mid h_0 (x) < 0\} $$ and $$ K_1 = \{x \in X_+ \mid h_0 (x) > 0\}. $$
nodes.statement_short: If $H_0$ meets $X_+$ only at $0$ we are done; otherwise split $X_+$ into the half-cones $K_0$ and $K_1$.

nodes.name: Find an internal point off $H_0$
nodes.statement: By assumptions there exists some $z \in \tint X_+$. We may assume that $z \notin H_0$, since otherwise we may replace $z$ with a convex combination of $z$ and some point in $X_+ \setminus H_0$ (we cannot have $X_+ \subset H_0$ since $X_+$ is assumed to be generating in $X$).
nodes.statement_short: Pick $z \in \tint X_+ \setminus H_0$, using that $X_+$ is generating.

nodes.name: Normalise the sign
nodes.statement: Therefore $$ z \in K_j = \{h_0 < 0\} \cap \tint X_+ = \tint K_j $$ for some $j \in \{0, 1\}$; by changing the sign of $h_0$ we may thus assume that $\tint K_0 \neq \emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: After a sign change of $h_0$ we may assume $\tint K_0 \neq \emptyset$.

nodes.name: Apply the separation proposition
nodes.statement: Applying Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep} yields a functional $f_0 \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ separating $K_0$ and $K_1$, and since the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$, it is easy to see that $H_0 = \{ x \mid f (x) = 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition regfuncsep separates $K_0$ and $K_1$ by a regular functional defining $H_0$.

nodes.name: Translate back
nodes.statement: Finally, $H = \{x \mid f (x) = f (x_0)\}$, and the proof of Proposition~\ref {regfunchp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Translating back gives $H$ as a level set of $f$.

nodes.name: Line-open difference of line-open convex sets
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is a linear space and $B \subset A \subset X$ are nonempty, convex and line-open, i.~e. $A = \tint A$ and $B = \tint B$. Then $A \setminus B \neq \emptyset$ implies that $\tint (A \setminus B) \neq \emptyset$; moreover, \begin {equation} A \cap \{z \mid g (z) > \alpha\} \subset \tint (A \setminus B) \end {equation} for some $g \in \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: If $A \setminus B$ is nonempty for nested line-open convex sets, it has internal points, and an open half-space slice of $A$ lies inside them.
assumptions: $X$ is a linear space and $B \subset A \subset X$ are nonempty, convex and line-open, i.~e. $A = \tint A$ and $B = \tint B$
conclusions: $A \setminus B \neq \emptyset$ implies that $\tint (A \setminus B) \neq \emptyset$
A \cap \{z \mid g (z) > \alpha\} \subset \tint (A \setminus B)

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition aocsd
nodes.statement: Indeed, let $y_0 \in A \setminus B$ and $x_0 \in \tint B$. By the standard separation theorem there exists a hyperplane $H = \{ y \mid g (y) = \alpha\}$ separating $y_0$ and $B$. By changing the sign of $g$ if necessary we may assume that $g (x_0) < \alpha$ and $g (y_0) \geqslant \alpha$. Since $A$ is line-open, there exists some $\lambda > 1$ such that $y = x_0 + \lambda (y_0 - x_0) \in A$. Therefore $g (y) = g (y_0) + (\lambda - 1) (g (y_0) - g (x_0)) > \alpha$. This means that $y$ belongs to the line-open set \eqref {aseplf}.
nodes.statement_short: Separate a point of $A \setminus B$ from $B$ by a hyperplane, then push past it along a line using line-openness of $A$.

nodes.name: Separate a point from $B$
nodes.statement: Indeed, let $y_0 \in A \setminus B$ and $x_0 \in \tint B$. By the standard separation theorem there exists a hyperplane $H = \{ y \mid g (y) = \alpha\}$ separating $y_0$ and $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $y_0 \in A \setminus B$ and an internal point of $B$, and separate them by a hyperplane.

nodes.name: Fix the orientation
nodes.statement: By changing the sign of $g$ if necessary we may assume that $g (x_0) < \alpha$ and $g (y_0) \geqslant \alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalise the sign of $g$ so that $g(x_0) < \alpha \leqslant g(y_0)$.

nodes.name: Push past the hyperplane
nodes.statement: Since $A$ is line-open, there exists some $\lambda > 1$ such that $y = x_0 + \lambda (y_0 - x_0) \in A$. Therefore $g (y) = g (y_0) + (\lambda - 1) (g (y_0) - g (x_0)) > \alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Line-openness of $A$ lets us move past $y_0$ to a point with $g(y) > \alpha$.

nodes.name: Conclude nonemptiness
nodes.statement: This means that $y$ belongs to the line-open set \eqref {aseplf}.
nodes.statement_short: The line-open set of the claim is nonempty.

nodes.name: RDP and $\mathcal L$-RDP coincide for line-open cones
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space satisfying $X_+ = \{0\} \cup \tint X_+$, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines and $Y$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $Y_+$ is generating for $Y$. Let $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ be a linear space of linear maps such that $y_0 \cdot \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L$ for some $y_0 \in Y$. Then the following conditions are equivalent. \begin {enumerate} \item $X$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property. \item $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. \end {enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For a generating, line-open cone of bounded aperture, the $\mathcal L$-RDP is equivalent to the classical RDP.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space satisfying $X_+ = \{0\} \cup \tint X_+$, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines
$Y$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $Y_+$ is generating for $Y$
$\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ be a linear space of linear maps such that $y_0 \cdot \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L$ for some $y_0 \in Y$
conclusions: $X$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property.
$X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem openlrdp
nodes.statement: Indeed, $1 \Rightarrow 2$ is trivial and so we only need to establish $2 \Rightarrow 1$. It is easy to see that we may, without loss of generality, assume that $Y = \mathbb R$ and $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L$ under the conditions of Proposition~\ref {openlrdp}. Suppose that $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property but there exist some $x, y, z \in X_+$ such that $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left([0, x] + [0, y]\right)$. Since by the assumptions $X_+ = \{0\} \cup \tint X_+$, we have $[0, x] = \{0\} \cup \tint [0, x]$ and thus $[0, x] + [0, y] = \{0\} \cup \tint \left( [0, x] + [0, y]\right)$. It is easy to see that $\tint [0, x] \neq \emptyset$ unless $X$ is trivial. Let $x_0 \in [0, x] + [0, y]$. Using Proposition~\ref {aocsd}, we may assume that \begin {equation} z \in A = \tint \left( [0, x + y] \setminus \left([0, x] + [0, y]\right) \right) \subset [0, x + y] \cap \{z \mid g (z) > \alpha\} \end {equation} with some linear functional $g$. Let $H = \{z \mid g (z) = \alpha\}$. Then by Proposition~\ref {regfunchp} there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $ H = \{a \mid f (a) = \beta\} $ with some $\beta \in \mathbb R$. This means that $f$ separates $A$ and $[0, x] + [0, y]$, and therefore strictly separates $z \in A = \tint A$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$, which contradicts the assumption that $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. The proof of Theorem~\ref {openlrdp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Assuming RDP fails, Proposition aocsd puts the offending $z$ in a line-open slice and Proposition regfunchp produces a regular functional that strictly separates it.

nodes.name: Only one implication is needed
nodes.statement: Indeed, $1 \Rightarrow 2$ is trivial and so we only need to establish $2 \Rightarrow 1$.
nodes.statement_short: $1 \Rightarrow 2$ is trivial, so only $2 \Rightarrow 1$ is proved.

nodes.name: Reduce to $Y = \mathbb R$
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that we may, without loss of generality, assume that $Y = \mathbb R$ and $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L$ under the conditions of Proposition~\ref {openlrdp}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce without loss of generality to $Y = \mathbb R$ with $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L$.

nodes.name: Assume RDP fails
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property but there exist some $x, y, z \in X_+$ such that $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left([0, x] + [0, y]\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the $\mathcal L$-RDP holds while some $z \in [0,x+y]$ lies outside $[0,x]+[0,y]$.

nodes.name: Order intervals are line-open
nodes.statement: Since by the assumptions $X_+ = \{0\} \cup \tint X_+$, we have $[0, x] = \{0\} \cup \tint [0, x]$ and thus $[0, x] + [0, y] = \{0\} \cup \tint \left( [0, x] + [0, y]\right)$. It is easy to see that $\tint [0, x] \neq \emptyset$ unless $X$ is trivial. Let $x_0 \in [0, x] + [0, y]$.
nodes.statement_short: Line-openness of the cone makes the order intervals and their sum line-open away from $0$.

nodes.name: Put $z$ in a line-open slice
nodes.statement: Using Proposition~\ref {aocsd}, we may assume that \begin {equation} z \in A = \tint \left( [0, x + y] \setminus \left([0, x] + [0, y]\right) \right) \subset [0, x + y] \cap \{z \mid g (z) > \alpha\} \end {equation} with some linear functional $g$. Let $H = \{z \mid g (z) = \alpha\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition aocsd places $z$ inside a line-open set cut out by a linear functional $g$.

nodes.name: Replace $g$ by a regular functional
nodes.statement: Then by Proposition~\ref {regfunchp} there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $ H = \{a \mid f (a) = \beta\} $ with some $\beta \in \mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition regfunchp realises the hyperplane $\{g = \alpha\}$ by a regular functional $f$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: This means that $f$ separates $A$ and $[0, x] + [0, y]$, and therefore strictly separates $z \in A = \tint A$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$, which contradicts the assumption that $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. The proof of Theorem~\ref {openlrdp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ strictly separates $z$ from $[0,x]+[0,y]$, contradicting the $\mathcal L$-RDP.

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich transform
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be ordered linear spaces, $n \geqslant 1$ and $T = \left\{T_1, \ldots, T_n\right\}$ be a finite collection of superlinear maps $T_j : X_+ \to Y$ for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$. The Riesz-Kantorovich transform $$ \rkts {T} = \rkts {T_1, \ldots, T_n} : x \mapsto \rkt {T} {x} $$ is defined by \begin {multline} \rkt {T} {x} = \rkt {T_1, \ldots, T_n} {x} = \\ \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \leqslant x \right\} \end {multline} for $x \in X_+$ whenever this supremum exists in $Y$. The positive Riesz-Kantorovich transform is defined by $$ \rktp {T} {x} = \rktp {T_1, \ldots, T_n} {x} = \rktp {0, T_1, \ldots, T_n} {x}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\rkts {T} (x)$ is the supremum of $\sum_j T_j (x_j)$ over decompositions with $\sum_j x_j \leqslant x$; the positive transform adds a zero map to the collection.
differentia: \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \leqslant x \right\}

nodes.name: The Riesz-Kantorovich transform is superlinear and order bounded
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that if maps $T_j$ are order bounded and $Y$ is Dedekind complete then the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkt {T} {x}$ is well-defined and $\rkts {T_1, \ldots, T_n} \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$. Since $[0, x] + [0, y] \subset [0, x + y]$ for all $x, y \in X_+$, it is easy to verify that $\rkts {T}$ is superadditive. Since the Riesz-Kantorovich transform is also positively homogeneous, we see that $\rkts {T}$ is a superlinear map that majorizes $T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$. Observe also that $\rkts {T}$ is order bounded whenever the operators from collection $T$ are.
nodes.statement_short: For order bounded $T_j$ and Dedekind complete $Y$, $\rkts {T}$ is a well-defined, order bounded superlinear majorant of every $T_j$.
conclusions: It is easy to see that if maps $T_j$ are order bounded and $Y$ is Dedekind complete then the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkt {T} {x}$ is well-defined and $\rkts {T_1, \ldots, T_n} \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$. Since $[0, x] + [0, y] \subset [0, x + y]$ for all $x, y \in X_+$, it is easy to verify that $\rkts {T}$ is superadditive. Since the Riesz-Kantorovich transform is also positively homogeneous, we see that $\rkts {T}$ is a superlinear map that majorizes $T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$. Observe also that $\rkts {T}$ is order bounded whenever the operators from collection $T$ are.

nodes.name: The transform is the infimum of superlinear majorants
nodes.statement: Suppose that under the assumptions of Definition~\ref {rktd} map $\rkts {T}$ is well-defined. Then \begin {multline} \rkts {T} = \\ \inf \{S : X_+ \to Y \mid \text {$S$ is superlinear and $S \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$}\}. \end {multline} In particular, $\rkts {T} = \bigvee_{j = 1}^n T_j$ in \suplinop {X_+} {Y}.
nodes.statement_short: $\rkts {T}$ is the least superlinear map dominating every $T_j$, i.e. their supremum in $\suplinop {X_+} {Y}$.
assumptions: under the assumptions of Definition~\ref {rktd} map $\rkts {T}$ is well-defined
conclusions: \inf \{S : X_+ \to Y \mid \text {$S$ is superlinear and $S \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$}\}
$\rkts {T} = \bigvee_{j = 1}^n T_j$ in \suplinop {X_+} {Y}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition rktinf
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref {rktinf} map $S : X_+ \to Y$ is superlinear and $S \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$. Then for any $x \in X_+$ and $x_j \in X_+$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, such that $\sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \leqslant x$, we have \begin {equation} S (x) \geqslant \sum_{j = 1}^n S (x_j) \geqslant \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \end {equation} by superadditivity of $S$, and \eqref {sssup} implies $S \geqslant \rkts {T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Superadditivity of any superlinear majorant $S$ bounds every admissible decomposition sum, hence $S \geqslant \rkts {T}$.

nodes.name: Take a superlinear majorant
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref {rktinf} map $S : X_+ \to Y$ is superlinear and $S \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$.
nodes.statement_short: Take any superlinear $S$ with $S \geqslant T_j$ for all $j$.

nodes.name: Superadditivity dominates every decomposition
nodes.statement: Then for any $x \in X_+$ and $x_j \in X_+$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, such that $\sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \leqslant x$, we have \begin {equation} S (x) \geqslant \sum_{j = 1}^n S (x_j) \geqslant \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \end {equation} by superadditivity of $S$, and \eqref {sssup} implies $S \geqslant \rkts {T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Superadditivity of $S$ dominates every admissible decomposition sum, so $S \geqslant \rkts {T}$.

nodes.name: Associativity of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $Y$ is Dedekind complete. Then for any order bounded superlinear maps $Q, R, S : X \to Y$ we have the relations \begin {equation} \rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S} = \rkts {Q, R, S} = \rkts {Q, \rkts {R, S}}. \end {equation}
nodes.statement_short: The transform of three order bounded superlinear maps is unchanged by any association of the arguments.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $Y$ is Dedekind complete
any order bounded superlinear maps $Q, R, S : X \to Y$
conclusions: \rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S} = \rkts {Q, R, S} = \rkts {Q, \rkts {R, S}}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition rkass
nodes.statement: By symmetry it is sufficient to establish the first equality in \eqref {asseq}. Observe that \eqref {rktinfrel} implies that $\rkts {Q, R, S} \geqslant \rkts {Q, R}$, and another application of Proposition~\ref {rktinf} yields $\rkts {Q, R, S} \geqslant \rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S}$. Let us verify the converse inequality. Suppose that $w \in X_+$. Then for any $x, y, z \in X_+$ such that $x + y + z \leqslant w$ we have $$ \rkt {\rkts {Q, R}, S} {w} \geqslant \rkt {Q, R} {x + y} + S (z) \geqslant Q (x) + R (y) + S (z), $$ so $\rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S} \geqslant \rkts {Q, R, S}$. It is easy to see that the Riesz-Kantorovich transform of any finite number of maps is stable under arbitrary association of terms in the spirit of Proposition~\ref {rkass}.
nodes.statement_short: One inequality follows from the infimum characterisation, the other by regrouping a three-term decomposition.

nodes.name: Reduce by symmetry
nodes.statement: By symmetry it is sufficient to establish the first equality in \eqref {asseq}.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry only the first equality has to be established.

nodes.name: One inequality from the infimum property
nodes.statement: Observe that \eqref {rktinfrel} implies that $\rkts {Q, R, S} \geqslant \rkts {Q, R}$, and another application of Proposition~\ref {rktinf} yields $\rkts {Q, R, S} \geqslant \rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S}$.
nodes.statement_short: The infimum characterisation gives $\rkts {Q,R,S} \geqslant \rkts {\rkts {Q,R}, S}$.

nodes.name: Regroup a decomposition
nodes.statement: Let us verify the converse inequality. Suppose that $w \in X_+$. Then for any $x, y, z \in X_+$ such that $x + y + z \leqslant w$ we have $$ \rkt {\rkts {Q, R}, S} {w} \geqslant \rkt {Q, R} {x + y} + S (z) \geqslant Q (x) + R (y) + S (z), $$ so $\rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S} \geqslant \rkts {Q, R, S}$. It is easy to see that the Riesz-Kantorovich transform of any finite number of maps is stable under arbitrary association of terms in the spirit of Proposition~\ref {rkass}.
nodes.statement_short: Regrouping $x + y + z \leqslant w$ gives the converse inequality.

nodes.name: Inequality in the definition cannot be replaced by equality
nodes.statement: Let us now briefly consider the question whether the inequality in the definition of \eqref {rktdef} can be replaced by an equality. A moment's reflection shows that it is generally not the case.

nodes.name: Supremum not attained at a full decomposition in $\mathbb R^3$
nodes.statement: For example, let $X = \mathbb R^3$ with the standard lattice order $X_+ = \left\{ (x, y, z) \mid x, y, z \geqslant 0 \right\}$ that appeared in Section~\ref {lrdps} above, and let $f ((x, y, z)) = -x + y - z$ and $g ((x, y, z)) = x - y - z$. Contemplating the extreme points of the order interval $[0, (x, y, z)]$ relative to the gradients $(-1, 1, -1)$ and $(1, -1, 1)$ of $f$ and $g$, one immediately notices that the supremum in \eqref {rktdef} for $\rkt {f, g} {(x, y, z)}$, $(x, y, z) \in X_+$, is attained at a decomposition $(0, y, 0) + (x, 0, 0)$, which is strictly smaller than $(x, y, z)$ in the order of $X$ unless $z = 0$, and that the corresponding supremum value $$ \rkt {f, g} {(x, y, z)} = x + y $$ would not have been attained had we replaced inequality in the definition \eqref {rktdef} by equality.
nodes.statement_short: For $f(x,y,z) = -x+y-z$ and $g(x,y,z) = x-y-z$ on $\mathbb R^3_+$ the optimal decomposition is strictly smaller than $x$ unless $z = 0$.

nodes.name: A positive member forces an exact decomposition
nodes.statement: However, it is easy to see that if one of the maps $T_j$ is positive then the supremum in \eqref {rktdef} is attained at some decomposition $\sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x$.
conclusions: However, it is easy to see that if one of the maps $T_j$ is positive then the supremum in \eqref {rktdef} is attained at some decomposition $\sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x$.

nodes.name: Equality form of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be ordered linear spaces, $n \geqslant 1$ and let $T = \left\{T_1, \ldots, T_n\right\}$ be a finite collection of linear maps $T_j : X_+ \to Y$ for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$. Suppose also that $T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$. Then \begin {multline} \rkt {T} {x} = \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x \right\}. \end {multline}
nodes.statement_short: If some $T_l$ is positive, the supremum may be taken over exact decompositions $\sum_j x_j = x$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ be ordered linear spaces, $n \geqslant 1$
$T = \left\{T_1, \ldots, T_n\right\}$ be a finite collection of linear maps $T_j : X_+ \to Y$ for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$
$T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$
conclusions: \rkt {T} {x} = \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x \right\}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition rkteq
nodes.statement: Indeed, the value of the right-hand part of \eqref {rktdefeq} is less or equal than $\rkt {T} {x}$ because the supremum is taken over a smaller set of decompositions. On the other hand, let $\sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \leqslant x$ be any decomposition in the definition \eqref {rktdef}. Then we can construct another decomposition $x = \sum_{j = 1}^n \tilde x_j$ by taking $\tilde x_j = x_j$ for $j \neq l$ and $\tilde x_l = x_l + \left[x - \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j\right]$ so that $ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (\tilde x_j) = \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) + T_l \left( x - \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \right) \geqslant \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j). $ It follows that \begin {multline*} \rkt {T} {x} \leqslant \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x \right\}, \end {multline*} which establishes \eqref {rktdefeq}.
nodes.statement_short: Absorb the slack $x - \sum_j x_j$ into the positive coordinate $T_l$, which cannot decrease the sum.

nodes.name: One inequality is immediate
nodes.statement: Indeed, the value of the right-hand part of \eqref {rktdefeq} is less or equal than $\rkt {T} {x}$ because the supremum is taken over a smaller set of decompositions.
nodes.statement_short: The exact-decomposition supremum is over a smaller set, hence at most $\rkt {T} {x}$.

nodes.name: Absorb the slack
nodes.statement: On the other hand, let $\sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \leqslant x$ be any decomposition in the definition \eqref {rktdef}. Then we can construct another decomposition $x = \sum_{j = 1}^n \tilde x_j$ by taking $\tilde x_j = x_j$ for $j \neq l$ and $\tilde x_l = x_l + \left[x - \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j\right]$ so that $ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (\tilde x_j) = \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) + T_l \left( x - \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \right) \geqslant \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j). $
nodes.statement_short: Add the slack $x - \sum_j x_j$ to the positive coordinate $x_l$ without decreasing the sum.

nodes.name: Conclude equality
nodes.statement: It follows that \begin {multline*} \rkt {T} {x} \leqslant \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x \right\}, \end {multline*} which establishes \eqref {rktdefeq}.
nodes.statement_short: Hence the two suprema coincide.

nodes.name: Reduction to the positive transform of a single map
nodes.statement: Propositions~\ref {rkass} and \ref {rktdefeq} allow us to reduce many questions regarding the general Reisz-Kantorovich transform to the case of $\rktps {T}$ of a single map $T$. Observe that \eqref {rktdefeq} implies that $$ \rkts {Q, R} = \rkts {0, Q - R} + R = \rktps {Q - R} + R $$ for a positive linear operator $R \geqslant 0$ and a superlinerar map $Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Associativity plus the equality form give $\rkts {Q,R} = \rktps {Q-R} + R$, reducing everything to $\rktps {T}$ of one map.
conclusions: Propositions~\ref {rkass} and \ref {rktdefeq} allow us to reduce many questions regarding the general Reisz-Kantorovich transform to the case of $\rktps {T}$ of a single map $T$. Observe that \eqref {rktdefeq} implies that $$ \rkts {Q, R} = \rkts {0, Q - R} + R = \rktps {Q - R} + R $$ for a positive linear operator $R \geqslant 0$ and a superlinerar map $Q$.

nodes.name: Stability of $\mathcal L$ under the transform of a collection
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be ordered linear spaces and $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ a linear space. Suppose that for any $T \in \mathcal L$ the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rktps {T}$ is well-defined and $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$. Then for any finite collection of operators $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$, $T_j \in \mathcal L$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, such that $T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$, we also have $\rkts {T} = \rkts {T_1, \ldots, T_n} \in \mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$ for every single $T \in \mathcal L$, the same holds for finite collections containing a positive member.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ be ordered linear spaces and $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ a linear space
for any $T \in \mathcal L$ the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rktps {T}$ is well-defined and $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$
$T_j \in \mathcal L$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, such that $T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$
conclusions: we also have $\rkts {T} = \rkts {T_1, \ldots, T_n} \in \mathcal L$

nodes.name: Linear transform is the supremum in the space of linear maps
nodes.statement: Since every linear map is superlinear, Proposition~\ref {rktinf} implies that if the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$ of a finite collection of \emph {linear} operators is well-defined and linear then $\rkts {T} = \bigvee_{j = 1}^n T_j$ in \linop {X_+} {Y} as well as in \suplinop {X_+} {Y}.
conclusions: Since every linear map is superlinear, Proposition~\ref {rktinf} implies that if the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$ of a finite collection of \emph {linear} operators is well-defined and linear then $\rkts {T} = \bigvee_{j = 1}^n T_j$ in \linop {X_+} {Y} as well as in \suplinop {X_+} {Y}.

nodes.name: $\mathcal L$-RDP is essentially linearity of the transform
nodes.statement: This leads to the Riesz-Kantorovich theorem mentioned in Section~\ref {anintroduction} as soon as one notices that the Riesz Decomposition Property of $X$ implies linearity of $\rktps {T}$ for any $T \in \blinop {X} {Y}$. More generally, it is not difficult to see that the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property introduced in Section~\ref {lrdps} above is, in many cases, essentially equivalent to linearity of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform. In the rest of the current section we explore the relationship between $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property and linearity of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform.

nodes.name: $\mathcal L$-RDP implies the transform stays in $\mathcal L$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice, $\mathcal L$ is a linear subspace of $\linop {X} {Y}$, $\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L$ and $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. Then for any finite collection of operators $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$ such that $T_j \in \mathcal L$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and $T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$, we also have $\rkts {T} \in \mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: If $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-RDP then $\rkts {T} \in \mathcal L$ for every finite collection containing a positive operator.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice, $\mathcal L$ is a linear subspace of $\linop {X} {Y}$, $\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L$ and $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property
$T_j \in \mathcal L$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and $T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$
conclusions: we also have $\rkts {T} \in \mathcal L$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition lrdptorkf
nodes.statement: Indeed, by Proposition~\ref {onlysing} it is sufficient to establish that for any $T \in \mathcal L$ the positive Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rktps {T}$ is linear; since $\rktps {T} \geqslant 0$, that would imply $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$ by the assumptions. Since $\rktps {T}$ is superlinear, we have $\rktp {T} {x + y} \geqslant \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}$ for all $x, y \in X_+$. Suppose that this inequality is strict for some $x, y \in X_+$. Then $y_0 = \rktp {T} {x + y} - \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y} > 0$, and from the definition of the supremum it follows that there exists some $z \in [0, x + y]$ such that \begin {equation} T z \geqslant \frac 1 2 y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y} \geqslant \frac 1 2 y_0 + T u + T v \end {equation} for all $u \in [0, x]$ and $v \in [0, y]$. But \eqref {tseplrdp} means that $T$ strictly separates $z \in [0, x + y]$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$, which contradicts the assumption that $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. This concludes the proof of Proposition~\ref {lrdptorkf}.
nodes.statement_short: Strict superadditivity of $\rktps {T}$ would let $T$ strictly separate a point of $[0,x+y]$ from $[0,x]+[0,y]$, contradicting the $\mathcal L$-RDP.

nodes.name: Reduce to a single map
nodes.statement: Indeed, by Proposition~\ref {onlysing} it is sufficient to establish that for any $T \in \mathcal L$ the positive Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rktps {T}$ is linear; since $\rktps {T} \geqslant 0$, that would imply $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$ by the assumptions.
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition onlysing it suffices to show $\rktps {T}$ is linear for a single $T$.

nodes.name: Superadditivity gives one inequality
nodes.statement: Since $\rktps {T}$ is superlinear, we have $\rktp {T} {x + y} \geqslant \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}$ for all $x, y \in X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Superlinearity already gives $\rktp {T} {x+y} \geqslant \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}$.

nodes.name: Assume strictness
nodes.statement: Suppose that this inequality is strict for some $x, y \in X_+$. Then $y_0 = \rktp {T} {x + y} - \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y} > 0$, and from the definition of the supremum it follows that there exists some $z \in [0, x + y]$ such that \begin {equation} T z \geqslant \frac 1 2 y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y} \geqslant \frac 1 2 y_0 + T u + T v \end {equation} for all $u \in [0, x]$ and $v \in [0, y]$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the inequality is strict and extract a $z \in [0, x+y]$ realising the gap.

nodes.name: Contradiction with the $\mathcal L$-RDP
nodes.statement: But \eqref {tseplrdp} means that $T$ strictly separates $z \in [0, x + y]$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$, which contradicts the assumption that $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. This concludes the proof of Proposition~\ref {lrdptorkf}.
nodes.statement_short: Then $T$ strictly separates $z$ from $[0,x]+[0,y]$, contradicting the $\mathcal L$-RDP.

nodes.name: Linearity of the transform implies the $\mathcal L$-RDP
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $\mathcal L$ is a linear subspace of $\linop {X} {Y}$. Suppose also that for any $T \in \mathcal L$ map $\rktps {T}$ is well-defined and linear. Then $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property.
nodes.statement_short: Converse of the previous proposition: linearity of $\rktps {T}$ for all $T \in \mathcal L$ forces the $\mathcal L$-RDP.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $\mathcal L$ is a linear subspace of $\linop {X} {Y}$
for any $T \in \mathcal L$ map $\rktps {T}$ is well-defined and linear
conclusions: Then $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition lrdp
nodes.statement: Suppose that, on the contrary, $X$ does not satisfy the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. This means that there exist some $x, y \in X_+$, $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left( [0, x] + [0, y]\right)$ and $T \in \mathcal L$ such that $T$ strictly separates $z$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$. By changing the sign of $T$ if necessary we may assume that \begin {equation} T z > \sup \{T (u + v) \mid u \in [0, x], v \in [0, y]\}. \end {equation} Let $y_0 = T z - \sup \{T (u + v) \mid u \in [0, x], v \in [0, y]\} > 0$. Then \eqref {tztuv} implies that \begin {equation} T z \geqslant y_0 + T u + T v \end {equation} for all $u \in [0, x]$ and $v \in [0, y]$. Taking supremums of the right-hand part of \eqref {tztuv2} one after the other yields \begin {multline*} T z \geqslant y_0 + \sup \{T u \mid u \in [0, x]\} + \sup \{T v \mid v \in [0, y]\} = \\ y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}, \end {multline*} which implies that \begin {equation} \rktp {T} {x + y} \geqslant T z \geqslant y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}. \end {equation} However, $\rktps {T}$ is linear by the assumptions, so $$ \rktp {T} {x + y} = \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}, $$ which contradicts \eqref {tztuv3} since $y_0 > 0$. The proof of Proposition~\ref {lrdp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: A strict separation of $z$ from $[0,x]+[0,y]$ by $T$ makes $\rktps {T}$ strictly superadditive, contradicting linearity.

nodes.name: Assume the $\mathcal L$-RDP fails
