nodes.statement: Suppose that, on the contrary, $X$ does not satisfy the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. This means that there exist some $x, y \in X_+$, $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left( [0, x] + [0, y]\right)$ and $T \in \mathcal L$ such that $T$ strictly separates $z$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the $\mathcal L$-RDP fails, giving $x, y, z$ and $T$ that strictly separates.

nodes.name: Normalise the sign
nodes.statement: By changing the sign of $T$ if necessary we may assume that \begin {equation} T z > \sup \{T (u + v) \mid u \in [0, x], v \in [0, y]\}. \end {equation}
nodes.statement_short: Normalise the sign of $T$ so that $T z$ exceeds the supremum over $[0,x]+[0,y]$.

nodes.name: Quantify the gap
nodes.statement: Let $y_0 = T z - \sup \{T (u + v) \mid u \in [0, x], v \in [0, y]\} > 0$. Then \eqref {tztuv} implies that \begin {equation} T z \geqslant y_0 + T u + T v \end {equation} for all $u \in [0, x]$ and $v \in [0, y]$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $y_0 > 0$ be the separation gap.

nodes.name: Take iterated suprema
nodes.statement: Taking supremums of the right-hand part of \eqref {tztuv2} one after the other yields \begin {multline*} T z \geqslant y_0 + \sup \{T u \mid u \in [0, x]\} + \sup \{T v \mid v \in [0, y]\} = \\ y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}, \end {multline*} which implies that \begin {equation} \rktp {T} {x + y} \geqslant T z \geqslant y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}. \end {equation}
nodes.statement_short: Taking suprema in $u$ and $v$ turns the gap into strict superadditivity of $\rktps {T}$.

nodes.name: Contradiction with linearity
nodes.statement: However, $\rktps {T}$ is linear by the assumptions, so $$ \rktp {T} {x + y} = \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}, $$ which contradicts \eqref {tztuv3} since $y_0 > 0$. The proof of Proposition~\ref {lrdp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: This contradicts the assumed linearity of $\rktps {T}$.

nodes.name: Dominating operator through an internal point
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space such that $x \in X_+$ is an internal point of $X_+$ and $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice. Suppose also that $p : X_+ \to Y$ is a superlinear map and $y \in Y$ satisfies $y \geqslant p (x)$. Then there exists a linear operator $M : X \to Y$ such that $M \geqslant p$ and $M x = y$.
nodes.statement_short: At an internal point $x$ of $X_+$, every value $y \geqslant p(x)$ is attained by some linear $M \geqslant p$.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space such that $x \in X_+$ is an internal point of $X_+$
$Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice
$p : X_+ \to Y$ is a superlinear map and $y \in Y$ satisfies $y \geqslant p (x)$
conclusions: there exists a linear operator $M : X \to Y$ such that $M \geqslant p$ and $M x = y$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma suprtli
nodes.statement: Indeed, observe that if $x$ is an internal point of $X_+$ (equivalently, an order unit of $X$) then the space $L = \{\alpha x \mid \alpha \in \mathbb R\}$ spanned by $x$ satisfies $X_+ + L = X$. Let $M_0 : \{\lambda x \mid \lambda > 0 \} \to Y$ be a map defined by $M_0 (\lambda x) = \lambda y$ for all $\lambda > 0$. Then $M_0 \geqslant p$ on the domain of $M_0$. We see that $M_0$ satisfies the conditions of the Hahn-Banach theorem (see Section~\ref {ovl}), and thus $M_0$ can be extended to a linear map $M$ satisfying the conclusion of Lemma~\ref {suprtli}.
nodes.statement_short: Define $M_0(\lambda x) = \lambda y$ on the ray through $x$ and extend it by the Hahn-Banach theorem.

nodes.name: The ray spans a valid domain
nodes.statement: Indeed, observe that if $x$ is an internal point of $X_+$ (equivalently, an order unit of $X$) then the space $L = \{\alpha x \mid \alpha \in \mathbb R\}$ spanned by $x$ satisfies $X_+ + L = X$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $x$ is an order unit, $L = \mathbb R x$ satisfies $X_+ + L = X$.

nodes.name: Define $M_0$ on the ray
nodes.statement: Let $M_0 : \{\lambda x \mid \lambda > 0 \} \to Y$ be a map defined by $M_0 (\lambda x) = \lambda y$ for all $\lambda > 0$. Then $M_0 \geqslant p$ on the domain of $M_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $M_0 (\lambda x) = \lambda y$, which dominates $p$ on its domain.

nodes.name: Extend by Hahn-Banach
nodes.statement: We see that $M_0$ satisfies the conditions of the Hahn-Banach theorem (see Section~\ref {ovl}), and thus $M_0$ can be extended to a linear map $M$ satisfying the conclusion of Lemma~\ref {suprtli}.
nodes.statement_short: The Hahn-Banach theorem extends $M_0$ to the required $M$.

nodes.name: Dominating continuous functional under a continuous superlinear map
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space equipped with a locally convex topology (not necessarily Hausdorff) such that the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$. Suppose also that $p : X_+ \to \mathbb R$ is a continuous superlinear map and points $x \in X_+$, $y \in \mathbb R$ satisfy $y > p (x)$. Then there exists a continous linear functional $M : X \to \mathbb R$ such that $M \geqslant p$ and $M (x) < y$.
nodes.statement_short: For a continuous superlinear $p$ on a generating cone and $y > p(x)$, there is a continuous linear $M \geqslant p$ with $M(x) < y$.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space equipped with a locally convex topology (not necessarily Hausdorff) such that the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$
$p : X_+ \to \mathbb R$ is a continuous superlinear map and points $x \in X_+$, $y \in \mathbb R$ satisfy $y > p (x)$
conclusions: there exists a continous linear functional $M : X \to \mathbb R$ such that $M \geqslant p$ and $M (x) < y$

nodes.name: Use separation instead of extension
nodes.statement: This lemma is a little more involved since we cannot in general just invoke the Hahn-Banach theorem in the absence of interior points; however, with a bit of topological reasoning we can instead make use of a separation theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Without interior points, replace the Hahn-Banach extension by a separation argument.

nodes.name: Form the subgraph and its closure
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma = \{ (z, t) \mid z \in X_+, t \leqslant p (x) \}$ be the subgraph of $p$, that is the epigraph of $-p$ turned upside down, and let $G = \bar \Gamma$ be its closure in $X \times \mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $\Gamma$ be the subgraph of $p$ and $G$ its closure in $X \times \mathbb R$.

nodes.name: $\Gamma$ is relatively closed
nodes.statement: Observe that since $p$ is continuous, $\Gamma$ is closed in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$ equipped with the relative topology induced by $X \times \mathbb R$. Indeed, for every $z \in X_+$ and $t \neq p (z)$ there exists a neighbourhood $V \subset X_+$ of $z$ such that $|p (a) - t| < \frac 1 2 |p (z) - t|$ for all $a \in V$; therefore $V \times (t - \frac 1 2 |p (z) - t|, t + \frac 1 2 |p (z) - t|)$ is an open neighbourhood of $(z, t)$ that does not intersect the graph $\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of $p$ makes $\Gamma$ closed in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$.

nodes.name: The closure adds nothing over $X_+$
nodes.statement: Closedness of $\Gamma$ in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$ implies that $G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R) = \Gamma$: inclusion $G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R) \supset \Gamma$ is trivial, and nonemptiness of $\left[G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R)\right] \setminus \Gamma$ would contradict relative closedness of $\Gamma$ in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$ since every point of $G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R)$ belongs to the closure of $\Gamma$ in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R) = \Gamma$.

i (x, y)$ that does not intersect $G$.
nodes.statement_short: So $(x,y) \notin G$ and a convex open $U \ni (x,y)$ misses $G$.

nodes.name: $G$ is a convex cone
nodes.statement: Superlinearity of $p$ implies that $\Gamma$ is a convex cone, and therefore $G$ is also a convex cone as a closure of a convex cone in the linear topological space $X \times \mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: Superlinearity makes $\Gamma$, hence $G$, a convex cone.

nodes.name: Take the conic hull of $U$
nodes.statement: Let $W = \bigcup_{\lambda > 0} \lambda U$ be the conic hull of $U$. $W$ is open because $U$ is open. Since $G$ is a cone and $U$ does not intersect $G$, it is easy to see that $W$ also does not intersect $G$.
nodes.statement_short: The conic hull $W$ of $U$ is open and still misses $G$.

nodes.name: Separate $G$ from $W$
nodes.statement: By the Hahn-Banach separation theorem there exists a linear functional $f : X \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ that separates $G$ and~$W$, that is $s = \sup \{f (b) \mid b \in G \} < f (c)$ for all $c \in W$. Since $W$ is open and nonempty, $f$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Hahn-Banach separation gives a continuous $f$ with $\sup_G f = s < f$ on $W$.

nodes.name: Read the hyperplane as a graph
nodes.statement: Now it remains to verify that $D = \{(z, t) \mid f ((z, t)) = s\}$ is a graph of a functional $M$ that satisfies the conclusion of Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0}.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show the level set $\{f = s\}$ is the graph of a functional $M$.

nodes.name: Vertical lines are surjective
nodes.statement: First, observe that $\{f ((z, t)) \mid t \in \mathbb R\} = \mathbb R$ for all $z \in X_+$: since by linearity $f ((z, t)) = f ((x, t)) + f ((z - x, 0))$, it is sufficient to establish that $f (x, \mathbb R) = \{f ((x, t)) \mid t \in \mathbb R\} = \mathbb R$, and this follows easily from the fact that $f (x, \mathbb R)$ is a linear subspace of $\mathbb R$ that cannot be trivial since $f ((x, p (x))) < f ((x, y))$. So $D$ is indeed a graph of a functional $M : X \to \mathbb R$, which is continuous since $f$ is continuous and therefore $D$ is closed.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is onto on every vertical line, so the level set is a graph.

nodes.name: $M$ is linear and continuous
nodes.statement: Linearity of $f$ implies that $M$ is affine, and from the fact that $f$ separates two cones it follows that $f (0, 0) = s$ and $M (0) = 0$, i.~e. $M$ is linear. Since the epigraph of $M$ contains an open set $U$, the epigraph of $M$ has nonempty interior and thus $M$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Linearity of $f$ and $f(0,0) = s$ make $M$ linear, and its epigraph has interior so $M$ is continuous.

nodes.name: Verify the two inequalities
nodes.statement: Finally, $M \geqslant p$ because $f ((z, p (z))) \leqslant s$ for all $z \in X_+$, and $M (x) < y$ because $f ((x, M (x))) = s < f ((x, y))$. The proof of Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Finally $M \geqslant p$ on $X_+$ and $M(x) < y$.

nodes.name: Continuity of the transform is needed to apply the lemma
nodes.statement: In order to apply Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0} to the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$ we need to make sure that $\rkts {T}$ is continuous as long as functionals $T$ are continuous.

nodes.name: Continuity of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear topological space. Then for any continuous linear functionals $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$, where $T_j : X \to \mathbb R$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$, assuming it is well-defined, is also continuous.
nodes.statement_short: The transform of finitely many continuous linear functionals is itself continuous wherever defined.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear topological space
any continuous linear functionals $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$, where $T_j : X \to \mathbb R$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$
conclusions: the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$, assuming it is well-defined, is also continuous

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition rktc
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that $\rkt {T} {x} = y$ for some $x \in X_+$ and $y \in \mathbb R$ and we are given an open neighbourhood $(y - \varepsilon, y + \varepsilon) \subset U \subset \mathbb R$ of $y$, $\varepsilon > 0$; we need to find an open neighbourhood $V \subset X_+$ of $x$ satisfying $\rkt {T} {V} \subset U$. Let $W = \left(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon\right) \subset \mathbb R$, so that $y + W \subset U$. Observe that a map $S : X^n \to \mathbb R$ defined by $S ((x_1, \ldots, x_n)) = \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j)$ is linear and continuous in $x_j \in X$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, as a composition of continuous maps. Moreover, $S$ is uniformly continuous because of its linearity, i.~e. there exists an open neighbourhood $V_1$ of $0$ such that \begin {equation} S ((x_1 + V_1, \ldots, x_n + V_1)) \subset S ((x_1, \ldots, x_n)) + W \end {equation} for all $x_j \in X$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$. Now let $V \subset X$ be an open balanced (i.~e. $V = -V$) neighbourhood of $0$ satisfying $V \subset V_1$. Inclusion \eqref {unicont} implies that \begin {equation} \rkt {T} {z_1} \geqslant \rkt {T} {z_0} - \varepsilon \end {equation} for all $z_0 \in X_+$ and $z_1 \in \left( z_0 + \sum_{k = 1}^n V \right) \cap X_+$. By setting $z_0 = x$ and $z_1 = x$ separately in \eqref {tzx} we arrive at the required continuity relation $|\rkt {T} {z} - \rkt {T} {x}| \leqslant \varepsilon$ for all $z \in x + \sum_{k = 1}^n V$. The proof of Proposition~\ref {rktc} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform continuity of $(x_1,\dots,x_n) \mapsto \sum_j T_j(x_j)$ transfers to the supremum, giving a two-sided $\varepsilon$-estimate.

nodes.name: Fix a target neighbourhood
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that $\rkt {T} {x} = y$ for some $x \in X_+$ and $y \in \mathbb R$ and we are given an open neighbourhood $(y - \varepsilon, y + \varepsilon) \subset U \subset \mathbb R$ of $y$, $\varepsilon > 0$; we need to find an open neighbourhood $V \subset X_+$ of $x$ satisfying $\rkt {T} {V} \subset U$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $x$, the value $y = \rkt {T} {x}$ and an $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of $y$.

nodes.name: Name the tolerance
nodes.statement: Let $W = \left(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon\right) \subset \mathbb R$, so that $y + W \subset U$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $W$ be the symmetric $\varepsilon$-interval.

nodes.name: The decomposition sum is continuous
nodes.statement: Observe that a map $S : X^n \to \mathbb R$ defined by $S ((x_1, \ldots, x_n)) = \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j)$ is linear and continuous in $x_j \in X$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, as a composition of continuous maps.
nodes.statement_short: The map $(x_1,\dots,x_n) \mapsto \sum_j T_j(x_j)$ is linear and continuous.

nodes.name: Uniform continuity
nodes.statement: Moreover, $S$ is uniformly continuous because of its linearity, i.~e. there exists an open neighbourhood $V_1$ of $0$ such that \begin {equation} S ((x_1 + V_1, \ldots, x_n + V_1)) \subset S ((x_1, \ldots, x_n)) + W \end {equation} for all $x_j \in X$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$.
nodes.statement_short: Linearity upgrades this to uniform continuity with a single neighbourhood $V_1$ of $0$.

nodes.name: Choose a balanced neighbourhood
nodes.statement: Now let $V \subset X$ be an open balanced (i.~e. $V = -V$) neighbourhood of $0$ satisfying $V \subset V_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a balanced $V \subset V_1$.

nodes.name: One-sided estimate
nodes.statement: Inclusion \eqref {unicont} implies that \begin {equation} \rkt {T} {z_1} \geqslant \rkt {T} {z_0} - \varepsilon \end {equation} for all $z_0 \in X_+$ and $z_1 \in \left( z_0 + \sum_{k = 1}^n V \right) \cap X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform continuity yields $\rkt {T} {z_1} \geqslant \rkt {T} {z_0} - \varepsilon$ nearby.

nodes.name: Symmetrise the estimate
nodes.statement: By setting $z_0 = x$ and $z_1 = x$ separately in \eqref {tzx} we arrive at the required continuity relation $|\rkt {T} {z} - \rkt {T} {x}| \leqslant \varepsilon$ for all $z \in x + \sum_{k = 1}^n V$. The proof of Proposition~\ref {rktc} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Applying the estimate in both directions gives the required continuity.

nodes.name: Archimedean ordered linear space
nodes.statement: Recall that an ordered linear space $Y$ is called \emph {Archimedean} if for any $y \in Y$ and $x \in Y_+$ inequalities $n y \leqslant x$ for all $n \geqslant 1$ imply that $y \leqslant 0$.
differentia: for any $y \in Y$ and $x \in Y_+$ inequalities $n y \leqslant x$ for all $n \geqslant 1$ imply that $y \leqslant 0$

nodes.name: The line-open cone induces the same order on operators
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $\tint X_+ \neq 0$. Suppose also that $Y$ is an Archimedean Dedekind complete lattice. Then $X$ ordered by $\{0\} \cup \tint X_+$ defines the same order in $\linop {X} {Y}$ as does $X$ ordered by $X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Ordering $X$ by $\{0\} \cup \tint X_+$ gives the same order on $\linop {X} {Y}$ as ordering it by $X_+$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $\tint X_+ \neq 0$
$Y$ is an Archimedean Dedekind complete lattice
conclusions: $X$ ordered by $\{0\} \cup \tint X_+$ defines the same order in $\linop {X} {Y}$ as does $X$ ordered by $X_+$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition isameorder
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that $T \in \linop {X} {Y}$ and $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in \tint X_+$ under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref {isameorder}; we need to verify that $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in X_+$. Fix any $x_0 \in \tint X_+$ and let $x_\theta = (1 - \theta) x_0 + \theta x$ for $0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 1$. Since $x_\theta \in \tint X_+$ for $0 \leqslant \theta < 1$, by the assumptions $T (x_\theta) \geqslant 0$ for $0 \leqslant \theta < 1$, and it suffices to verify that $T (x_1) \geqslant 0$. Since $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice, there exists $y_\alpha = \inf \{T (x_\theta) \mid \alpha \leqslant \theta < 1\}$ for all $0 \leqslant \alpha < 1$ and $y_\alpha \geqslant 0$. Linearity of $T (x_\theta)$ in $\theta$ implies that $$ T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) \leqslant T (x_\theta) \leqslant T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) $$ for all $\alpha \leqslant \theta \leqslant 1$, so \begin {equation} 0 \vee [T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)] \leqslant y_\alpha \leqslant T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) \end {equation} for all $0 < \alpha < 1$. Now observe that linearity of $T (x_\theta)$ in $\theta$ also implies that the set-valued map $\alpha \mapsto \{y \in Y \mid y \geqslant T (x_\alpha), y \geqslant T (x_1)\}$ is affine in $0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant 1$, so $\alpha \mapsto T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1)$ and likewise $\alpha \mapsto T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)$ are affine in $0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant 1$; therefore $\varphi (\alpha) = T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) - T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)$ is an affine positive map and $\varphi (1) = 0$. In particular, $$ T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) = T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) + \varphi (\alpha) \leqslant T (x_1) + \varphi (0), $$ so the set of values of the right-hand part of \eqref {veeest} has an upper bound. Let $$ m_1 = \sup \{T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\}, $$ $$ y_1 = \sup \{y_\alpha \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\} $$ and $$ M_1 = \inf \{T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\}. $$ It is easy to see that $0 \leqslant m_1 \leqslant y_1 \leqslant M_1$; moreover, $$ M_1 - m_1 \leqslant \varphi (\alpha) = (1 - \alpha) \varphi (0) $$ for all $0 \leqslant \alpha < 1$, so the Archimedean property of $Y$ implies that $M_1 - m_1 \leqslant 0$, and thus $0 \leqslant m_1 = y_1 = M_1$. Furthermore, $$ m_1 \leqslant T (x_1) \leqslant M_1, $$ which implies that $m_1 = M_1 = T (x_1)$, and therefore $y_1 = T (x_1) \geqslant 0$. The proof of Proposition~\ref {isameorder} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Approach $x$ along a segment from an internal point and squeeze $T(x_1)$ between affine lattice bounds, closing the gap by the Archimedean property.

nodes.name: Reduce to a single $x$
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that $T \in \linop {X} {Y}$ and $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in \tint X_+$ under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref {isameorder}; we need to verify that $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $T \geqslant 0$ on $\tint X_+$ and verify $T x \geqslant 0$ for arbitrary $x \in X_+$.

nodes.name: Segment from an internal point
nodes.statement: Fix any $x_0 \in \tint X_+$ and let $x_\theta = (1 - \theta) x_0 + \theta x$ for $0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Join an internal point $x_0$ to $x$ by the segment $x_\theta$.

nodes.name: Positivity along the open segment
nodes.statement: Since $x_\theta \in \tint X_+$ for $0 \leqslant \theta < 1$, by the assumptions $T (x_\theta) \geqslant 0$ for $0 \leqslant \theta < 1$, and it suffices to verify that $T (x_1) \geqslant 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $T(x_\theta) \geqslant 0$ for $\theta < 1$, so only the endpoint is at issue.

nodes.name: Tail infima
nodes.statement: Since $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice, there exists $y_\alpha = \inf \{T (x_\theta) \mid \alpha \leqslant \theta < 1\}$ for all $0 \leqslant \alpha < 1$ and $y_\alpha \geqslant 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Dedekind completeness gives tail infima $y_\alpha \geqslant 0$.

nodes.name: Sandwich the tail infima
nodes.statement: Linearity of $T (x_\theta)$ in $\theta$ implies that $$ T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) \leqslant T (x_\theta) \leqslant T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) $$ for all $\alpha \leqslant \theta \leqslant 1$, so \begin {equation} 0 \vee [T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)] \leqslant y_\alpha \leqslant T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) \end {equation} for all $0 < \alpha < 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Linearity in $\theta$ sandwiches $y_\alpha$ between lattice combinations of $T(x_\alpha)$ and $T(x_1)$.

nodes.name: The gap is affine and vanishes at $1$
nodes.statement: Now observe that linearity of $T (x_\theta)$ in $\theta$ also implies that the set-valued map $\alpha \mapsto \{y \in Y \mid y \geqslant T (x_\alpha), y \geqslant T (x_1)\}$ is affine in $0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant 1$, so $\alpha \mapsto T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1)$ and likewise $\alpha \mapsto T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)$ are affine in $0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant 1$; therefore $\varphi (\alpha) = T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) - T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)$ is an affine positive map and $\varphi (1) = 0$. In particular, $$ T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) = T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) + \varphi (\alpha) \leqslant T (x_1) + \varphi (0), $$ so the set of values of the right-hand part of \eqref {veeest} has an upper bound.
nodes.statement_short: The gap $\varphi(\alpha)$ between the two bounds is affine, positive and vanishes at $\alpha = 1$.

nodes.name: Name the three limits
nodes.statement: Let $$ m_1 = \sup \{T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\}, $$ $$ y_1 = \sup \{y_\alpha \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\} $$ and $$ M_1 = \inf \{T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $m_1$, $y_1$ and $M_1$ as the extreme values of the bounds.

nodes.name: Archimedean squeeze
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that $0 \leqslant m_1 \leqslant y_1 \leqslant M_1$; moreover, $$ M_1 - m_1 \leqslant \varphi (\alpha) = (1 - \alpha) \varphi (0) $$ for all $0 \leqslant \alpha < 1$, so the Archimedean property of $Y$ implies that $M_1 - m_1 \leqslant 0$, and thus $0 \leqslant m_1 = y_1 = M_1$.
nodes.statement_short: The Archimedean property forces $M_1 - m_1 \leqslant 0$, so all three coincide.

nodes.name: Identify the common value
nodes.statement: Furthermore, $$ m_1 \leqslant T (x_1) \leqslant M_1, $$ which implies that $m_1 = M_1 = T (x_1)$, and therefore $y_1 = T (x_1) \geqslant 0$. The proof of Proposition~\ref {isameorder} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Since $T(x_1)$ lies between them, $T(x_1) = y_1 \geqslant 0$.

nodes.name: Dedekind completeness cannot be dropped
nodes.statement: We mention that Poposition~\ref {isameorder} may fail without the assumption that $Y$ is Dedekind complete; it is easy to construct a finite-dimensional example with some closed $X_+$ and open $Y_+$.

nodes.name: Is the Archimedean assumption necessary?
nodes.statement: It is, however, not clear whether the assumption that $Y$ is Archimedean is necessary for the conclusion of Proposition~\ref {isameorder}.
nodes.statement_short: Whether Proposition isameorder needs $Y$ Archimedean is left open.

nodes.name: Characterise linearity of the transform via existence of suprema
nodes.statement: As it was explained in Section~\ref {ovl}, there is a long-standing open problem that can be rephrased as follows: is it possible to characterize linearity of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform of a particular finite collection $T$ of linear operators in terms of the existence of the supremum of $T$ in an ordered space of linear operators?
nodes.statement_short: Can linearity of $\rkts {T}$ be characterised by existence of $\sup T$ in an ordered space of operators?
nodes.origin_citation: Aliprantis & Burkinshaw, Positive Operators, §2; Aliprantis & Tourky 2002

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich formula for continuous functionals
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered locally convex linear topological space, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$ and $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$. Then for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L = \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ we have $\sup T = \rkts {T}$.
nodes.statement_short: If a supremum of continuous functionals exists in $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, it equals the Riesz-Kantorovich transform.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered locally convex linear topological space, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$ and $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$
any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L = \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$
conclusions: we have $\sup T = \rkts {T}$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem suprtc
nodes.statement: Suppose that under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref {suprt} $T \subset \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ is a finite collection of functionals such that the supremum of $T$ exists in $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$. Let us denote this supremum by $S = \sup T$; we need to verify that $S = \rkts {T}$. Observe that from Proposition~\ref {rktinf} it follows that $\rkts {T} \leqslant S$. Now suppose that $\rkts {T} = S$ does not hold true, which means that there exists some $x \in X_+$ such that $\rkt {T} {x} < S (x)$. By Proposition~\ref {rktc} the Riesz-Kantorovich trasform $\rkts {T}$ is continuous, and since it is superlinear we can apply Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0} to points $x$ and $y = S (x)$ with $p = \rkts {T}$ to obtain a linear continuous functional $M \geqslant \rkts {T}$ satisfying $M (x) < S (x)$. However, $S = \sup T$ implies that $S \leqslant M$ since $M \geqslant \rkts {T} \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, and therefore $M (x) \geqslant \sup T (x) = S (x)$. This contradiction concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprtc}.
nodes.statement_short: If $\rkts {T} < S$ somewhere, Lemma suprtlf0 produces a continuous majorant $M$ of $\rkts {T}$ with $M(x) < S(x)$, contradicting $S = \sup T$.

nodes.name: Take an existing supremum
nodes.statement: Suppose that under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref {suprt} $T \subset \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ is a finite collection of functionals such that the supremum of $T$ exists in $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a finite $T$ whose supremum exists in $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$.

nodes.name: Name the supremum
nodes.statement: Let us denote this supremum by $S = \sup T$; we need to verify that $S = \rkts {T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $S = \sup T$; the claim is $S = \rkts {T}$.

nodes.name: One inequality
nodes.statement: Observe that from Proposition~\ref {rktinf} it follows that $\rkts {T} \leqslant S$.
nodes.statement_short: The infimum characterisation gives $\rkts {T} \leqslant S$.

nodes.name: Assume a strict gap
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $\rkts {T} = S$ does not hold true, which means that there exists some $x \in X_+$ such that $\rkt {T} {x} < S (x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\rkt {T} {x} < S(x)$ for some $x \in X_+$.

nodes.name: Produce a smaller majorant
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref {rktc} the Riesz-Kantorovich trasform $\rkts {T}$ is continuous, and since it is superlinear we can apply Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0} to points $x$ and $y = S (x)$ with $p = \rkts {T}$ to obtain a linear continuous functional $M \geqslant \rkts {T}$ satisfying $M (x) < S (x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of $\rkts {T}$ plus Lemma suprtlf0 give a continuous $M \geqslant \rkts {T}$ with $M(x) < S(x)$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: However, $S = \sup T$ implies that $S \leqslant M$ since $M \geqslant \rkts {T} \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, and therefore $M (x) \geqslant \sup T (x) = S (x)$. This contradiction concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprtc}.
nodes.statement_short: But $M$ majorises every $T_j$, so $S \leqslant M$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich formula for order bounded functionals
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear topological space, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, and $\mathcal L$ is a linear space of linear functionals satisfying $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$. Then for any finite collection $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L$ we have $\sup T = \rkts {T}$.
nodes.statement_short: The same conclusion holds for any $\mathcal L$ between the regular and the order bounded functionals.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear topological space, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, and $\mathcal L$ is a linear space of linear functionals satisfying $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$
any finite collection $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L$
conclusions: we have $\sup T = \rkts {T}$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem suprtf
nodes.statement: Indeed, observe that the supremum $S = \sup T$ in $\mathcal L$ is also a supremum of $T$ in $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, since any upper bound $U \in \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ of $T$ also belongs to $\mathcal L$ because $U \geqslant T_1$, so $U - T_1 \geqslant 0$ and $U$ is a sum of $T_1 \in \mathcal L$ and a regular operator $U - T_1$. Equipping $X$ with its order topology (see Section~\ref {ovl}) reduces Theorem~\ref {suprtf} at once to a direct application of Theorem~\ref {suprtc}.
nodes.statement_short: Upper bounds in $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ already lie in $\mathcal L$, so the order topology reduces the claim to Theorem suprtc.

nodes.name: The supremum is absolute
nodes.statement: Indeed, observe that the supremum $S = \sup T$ in $\mathcal L$ is also a supremum of $T$ in $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, since any upper bound $U \in \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ of $T$ also belongs to $\mathcal L$ because $U \geqslant T_1$, so $U - T_1 \geqslant 0$ and $U$ is a sum of $T_1 \in \mathcal L$ and a regular operator $U - T_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Any upper bound in $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ lies in $\mathcal L$, so $S$ is also the supremum there.

nodes.name: Reduce to the continuous case
nodes.statement: Equipping $X$ with its order topology (see Section~\ref {ovl}) reduces Theorem~\ref {suprtf} at once to a direct application of Theorem~\ref {suprtc}.
nodes.statement_short: In the order topology the statement is exactly Theorem suprtc.

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich formula at internal points for operators
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, $X_+$ has an internal point, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice and $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ is a linear space of linear operators acting from $X$ to $Y$ satisfying $ \rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {Y}. $ Then for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L$ we have $\sup T (x) = \rkt {T} {x}$ for all $x \in \tint X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: For operators into a Dedekind complete lattice with $X_+$ having an internal point, an existing supremum agrees with the transform on $\tint X_+$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, $X_+$ has an internal point, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice
\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {Y}
any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L$
conclusions: we have $\sup T (x) = \rkt {T} {x}$ for all $x \in \tint X_+$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem suprt
nodes.statement: The proof essentially repeats the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprtc} above with only a couple of small twists. Suppose that $T \subset \mathcal L$ is a finite collection of operators under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref {suprt} such that the supremum of $T$ exists in $\mathcal L$. We denote this supremum by $S = \sup T$ and it is set upon us to verify that $S = \rkts {T}$ on the set of all internal points of $X_+$. From Proposition~\ref {rktinf} it follows that $\rkts {T} \leqslant S$. Suppose that $\rkt {T} {x} = S (x)$ does not hold true for all $x \in \tint X_+$. Then there exists some $x \in \tint X_+$ such that $\rkt {T} {x} < S (x)$. Let $y = \frac 1 2 \left( \rkt {T} {x} + S (x) \right)$; then $\rkt {T} {x} < y < S (x)$. By Lemma~\ref {suprtli} there exists a linear map $M \in \linop {X} {Y}$ such that $M \geqslant \rkts {T}$ and $M (x) = y < S (x)$. Observe that $M \geqslant T_1$, so $M - T_1 \in \rlinop {X} {Y}$ and therefore $M \in \rlinop {X} {Y} + \mathcal L = \mathcal L$. However, $S = \sup T$ in $\mathcal L$ implies that $S \leqslant M$, so $M (x) \geqslant S (x)$. This contradiction concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprt}.
nodes.statement_short: Same contradiction as for Theorem suprtc, with Lemma suprtli supplying a linear $M$ that takes an intermediate value at an internal point.

nodes.name: Reuse the previous argument
nodes.statement: The proof essentially repeats the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprtc} above with only a couple of small twists. Suppose that $T \subset \mathcal L$ is a finite collection of operators under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref {suprt} such that the supremum of $T$ exists in $\mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: The argument copies the proof of Theorem suprtc with small changes.

nodes.name: Name the supremum
nodes.statement: We denote this supremum by $S = \sup T$ and it is set upon us to verify that $S = \rkts {T}$ on the set of all internal points of $X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $S = \sup T$ and aim at $S = \rkts {T}$ on $\tint X_+$.

nodes.name: One inequality
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref {rktinf} it follows that $\rkts {T} \leqslant S$.
nodes.statement_short: The infimum characterisation gives $\rkts {T} \leqslant S$.

nodes.name: Assume a strict gap
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\rkt {T} {x} = S (x)$ does not hold true for all $x \in \tint X_+$. Then there exists some $x \in \tint X_+$ such that $\rkt {T} {x} < S (x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\rkt {T} {x} < S(x)$ at some internal point $x$.

nodes.name: Pick an intermediate value
nodes.statement: Let $y = \frac 1 2 \left( \rkt {T} {x} + S (x) \right)$; then $\rkt {T} {x} < y < S (x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $y$ strictly between $\rkt {T} {x}$ and $S(x)$.

nodes.name: Build a dominating operator
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref {suprtli} there exists a linear map $M \in \linop {X} {Y}$ such that $M \geqslant \rkts {T}$ and $M (x) = y < S (x)$. Observe that $M \geqslant T_1$, so $M - T_1 \in \rlinop {X} {Y}$ and therefore $M \in \rlinop {X} {Y} + \mathcal L = \mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma suprtli gives a linear $M \geqslant \rkts {T}$ with $M(x) = y < S(x)$, and $M \in \mathcal L$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: However, $S = \sup T$ in $\mathcal L$ implies that $S \leqslant M$, so $M (x) \geqslant S (x)$. This contradiction concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprt}.
nodes.statement_short: But $S \leqslant M$ forces $M(x) \geqslant S(x)$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Is the transform linear on all of $X_+$?
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, it does not seem to be clear whether $\rkts {T}$ is linear on all $X_+$ under the conditions of Theorem~\ref {suprt}.
nodes.statement_short: Whether $\rkts {T}$ is linear on the whole cone $X_+$ under the hypotheses of Theorem suprt is left open.

nodes.name: The gap does not obstruct the applications
nodes.statement: Luckily, however, this omission in our understanding of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform does not get in the way of the applications connecting the properties of $X$ and $\mathcal L$, since the operators in $\mathcal L$ are uniquely defined by their values on $\tint X_+$.

nodes.name: Replacing existence of suprema by the RDP
nodes.statement: Let us now observe that in the same three cases treated in Theorems~\ref {suprtc}--\ref {suprt} above we can replace the assumption that $\sup S$ exists in $\mathcal L$ by the assumption that $\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property and still arrive at the corresponding linearity of $\rkts {T}$. We will only prove it for the two cases that are used in Theorem~\ref {grkf} below.
nodes.statement_short: The hypothesis that $\sup T$ exists may be replaced by the RDP of $\mathcal L$ in all three settings.

nodes.name: RDP of a functional space makes the transform stay inside
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, and $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ is a linear space of linear functionals on $X$ satisfying $ \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}. $ Suppose also that $\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property. Then $\rkts {T} \in \mathcal L$ for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: If a space of functionals between the regular and order bounded ones has the RDP, it is closed under the Riesz-Kantorovich transform.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$
\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}
$\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property
conclusions: Then $\rkts {T} \in \mathcal L$ for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$

nodes.name: RDP of an operator space makes the transform linear on internal points
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, $X_+$ has an internal point, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice and $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ is a linear space of linear operators acting from $X$ to $Y$ satisfying $ \rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {Y}. $ Suppose also that $\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property. Then $\rkts {T}$ is linear on $\tint X_+$ for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$, and the unique extension of $\rkts {T}$ restricted to $\tint X_+$ to a linear operator from $\linop {X} {Y}$ belongs to~$\mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\mathcal L$ has the RDP then $\rkts {T}$ is linear on $\tint X_+$ and its linear extension stays in $\mathcal L$.

nodes.name: Proof of Propositions suprtrdp and suprtrdpf
nodes.statement: We will now give a proof for Proposition~\ref {suprtrdp} that also works as a proof of Proposition~\ref {suprtrdpf} with suitable apparent minor modifications. Indeed, under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref {suprtrdp} the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$ is well-defined and superlinear. Suppose that it is not linear on $\tint X_+$; this means that $\rkt {T} {x + y} > \rkt {T} {x} + \rkt {T} {y}$ for some $x, y \in \tint X_+$. Let $z = \rkt {T} {x + y} - \left[\rkt {T} {x} + \rkt {T} {y} \right] > 0$. By Lemma~\ref {suprtli} we can find some $S_0, S_1 \in \linop {X} {Y}$ such that $S_0, S_1 \geqslant \rkts {T}$ and \begin {equation} S_0 (x) = \rkt {T} {x} + \frac 1 4 z, \quad S_1 (y) = \rkt {T} {y} + \frac 1 4 z. \end {equation} By the same reasoning as in the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprt} we have $S_0, S_1 \in \mathcal L$. Since by the assumption $\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property, it also has the interpolation property (see Section~\ref {ovl}). Observe that $\{S_0, S_1\} \geqslant \rkts {T} \geqslant T$, so $\{S_0, S_1\} \geqslant T$, and by the interpolation property of $\mathcal L$ there exists some $S \in \mathcal L$ such that $\{S_0, S_1\} \geqslant S \geqslant T$. Therefore $S \geqslant \rkts {T}$ by Proposition~\ref {rktinf}. It follows that \begin {multline} S (x + y) - [S (x) + S (y)] \geqslant \rkt {T} {x + y} -[S_0 (x) + S_1 (y)] = \\ \left(\rkt {T} {x + y} - \left[\rkt {T} {x} + \rkt {T} {y} \right]\right) - \frac 1 2 z = z - \frac 1 2 z = \frac 1 2 z > 0, \end {multline} so $S$ cannot be linear. This contradiction concludes the proof of Proposition~\ref {suprtrdp}. In order to prove Proposition~\ref {suprtrdpf} we modify this proof as follows. Surely we need to take any $x, y \in X_+$ and not just $x, y \in \tint X_+$. As in the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprtf} we equip $X$ with its order topology. Then Lemma~\ref {suprtrdpf} instead of Lemma~\ref {suprtli} gives $S_0$ and $S_1$ satisfying inequalities $<$ in \eqref {s0s1} rather than equalities, and thus we get inequality $>$ instead of the first equality in \eqref {sestrk}. The rest of the proof does not change.
nodes.statement_short: Strict superadditivity gives two operators above $\rkts {T}$ that the interpolation property interpolates, producing a non-linear $S$ in $\mathcal L$ — a contradiction.

nodes.name: Exact form of the Riesz-Kantorovich theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, $X_+$ is a generating cone in $X$, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice and $\mathcal L$ is a linear space of operators from $X$ to $Y$ satisfying $\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {Y}$. Suppose also that either the following assumptions is satisfied. \begin {enumerate} \item $Y = \mathbb R$; we set $X_r = X_+$ in this case. \item $\tint X_+ \neq \emptyset$ and $Y$ is Archimedean; we set $X_r = \{0\} \cup \tint X_+$ in this case. \end {enumerate} Then the following conditions are equivalent. \begin {enumerate} \item $\mathcal L$ is a lattice. \item $\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property. \item The Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$ of any finite collection~$T$ of operators from $\mathcal L$ is linear on $X_r$. \item For any operator $T \in \mathcal L$ the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rktps {T}$ is linear on $X_r$. \item $X$ ordered by the cone $X_r$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. \end {enumerate} Moreover, if any (and therefore all) of these conditions are satisfied then $\mathcal L = \rlinop {X} {Y}$ and $\sup T = \rkts {T}$ in $\mathcal L$ on $X_r$ for any finite collection of operators $T \subset \mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\mathcal L$ between the regular and order bounded operators, being a lattice, having the RDP, linearity of the transform, and the $\mathcal L$-RDP are all equivalent — and then $\mathcal L = \rlinop {X} {Y}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem grkf
nodes.statement: It is well known that implication $1 \Rightarrow 2$ is satisfied for any ordered linear space $\mathcal L$. Implication $2 \Rightarrow 3$ follows from either Proposition~\ref {suprtrdpf} or Proposition~\ref {suprtrdp}. Implication $3 \Rightarrow 4$ is trivial. Observe that the cone $X_r$ is generating for $X$, and by Proposition~\ref {isameorder} space $X$ ordered by $X_r$ generates the same order in $\linop {X} {Y}$ as does $X$ ordered by $X_+$. Proposition~\ref {lrdp} proves the implication $4 \Rightarrow 5$. Suppose now that Condition~5 of Theorem~\ref {grkf} is staisfied. Then Proposition~\ref {lrdptorkf} implies that for any $T \in \mathcal L$ we have $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$, and from Proposition~\ref {rktinf} it follows that $\rktps {T} = T^+ = T \vee 0$ in $\mathcal L$, so $\mathcal L$ is a lattice (since then for any $S, T \in \mathcal L$ expression $(T - S)^+ + S$ provides the supremum $S \vee T$ of $\{S, T\}$). We have thus verified implication $5 \Rightarrow 1$. Finally, if Condition~1 is satisfied then for any $T \in \mathcal L$ we have a decomposition $T = T \vee 0 - (-T) \vee 0$ into a difference of two positive linear maps that belong to $\mathcal L$, so $\mathcal L \subset \rlinop {X} {Y}$, and the converse inclusion was assumed. Thus $\mathcal L = \rlinop {X} {Y}$. Of course, Condition~1 means that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L$ for a finite $T \subset \mathcal L$, so $\sup T = \rkts {T}$ follows from either Theorem~\ref {suprtf} or Theorem~\ref {suprt}. The proof of Theorem~\ref {grkf} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Close the cycle $1 \Rightarrow 2 \Rightarrow 3 \Rightarrow 4 \Rightarrow 5 \Rightarrow 1$ using the propositions of the previous sections, then read off $\mathcal L = \rlinop {X} {Y}$.
